title: QB Carson Beck  Press Conference | Arizona Cardinals 2026
text: How OTAs and mandatory minicamp went for you from your perspective? >> Yeah, I mean, I thought it's been good. You know, it's it's been really good just getting adjusted to, you know, moving out to Arizona, meeting my new teammates, coaches, right? Um you know, the last time I got to talk in front of y'all, I had literally been here for like 2 hours, you know, and now it's been 6 weeks, so I've had a little time to, you know, get settled down and, you know, really get some good work in. So, I thought it's been really good. >> At that point you said you were kind of just getting your your feet wet with the playbook and kind of getting into it. Where do you feel like you're at now compared to there in terms of your understanding of the system and just your kind of comfort level with everything that goes into being an NFL quarterback? >> Well, yeah, I mean, completely different, obviously, you know, having 6 weeks where really all I've done is been here at home and then, you know, eating sleep cuz that's pretty necessary as well, you know, being a football player, but uh really that's that's all I've done, you know, I've been been here at time, been around the guys, been around the coaches, you know, meeting and trying to learn everything as as quick as possible. So, obviously, the the playbook is big, you know, there there is a lot of things to learn, but you know, the more time that I spend and the more reps you get, the more comfortable you get with it and the more it just kind of feels like you're looking at the back of your hand. >> So, do you feel like you're at 100% there or is there still kind of a few things to to work out? >> I think the cool thing about football and something that I've learned even over the, you know, past 3 years that I got to start in college is that there's always room for growth, especially as a quarterback, but in any position and in the playbook as well. Like when you get into a new playbook and even just a new year in general, right? And this is kind of what I had to learn at Georgia because being there for 5 years and having the essentially the same playbook for 5 years, you have to find ways to learn and grow in that playbook, even though you're doing the same thing over and over and over again, right? You you can't get bored with doing the simple things. You can't get bored with doing the basics. So, how good can you get at doing the simple things at getting all the way to the last progression and checking the ball down, taking your first read when they drop out in zone and taking 7 yd on first down, right? There's so many different things that accumulate to create the quarterback position, but in this, you know, case in this offense is hey, okay, let's learn the plays. Yeah, I think I have that down. Okay, now we have to hear coach LaFleur say it in the helmet, right? That's a new voice, right? I had coach Dawson last year saying it in my helmet, so let's get used to his voice. Now, let's go into the huddle and talk to new guys, lead new guys, right? Um demand the huddle. Um so again, there's so much that comes with being a quarterback, but I feel like I've really, you know, gotten a good grasp on it, you know, through this um this past 6 weeks and there's going to be more room to grow as we head into training camp. >> Coach LaFleur had said that you asked him a mature question as far as like ball placement or velo recently. Do you feel like you've checked enough boxes? Do you feel comfortable now as like, all right, I want to prove I can catch up with the game speed that coach Hackett talks about? You're ready to kind of prove yourself from that standpoint? >> Again, I I think the biggest thing in especially in the first couple of weeks that I noticed, you know, heading into this is A, the the NFL game is 100% different than the college game, right? We I mean, there's different routes that they're running. There's different concepts in the way that we piece everything together. So, A, where do I where do my eyes need to be, right? Um where are the defenders, right? Like, what coverages are they running? Everything is disguised, especially in today's NFL. I feel like it's very different what defenses are doing, how athletic these guys are, right? The these defensive linemen and especially the edge guys, you know, there's a lot of stand-up guys that can do a lot and are very versatile. So, defenses are able to do more, right? So, I need to make sure my eyes are in the right place. I need to make sure I understand who's running what route, right? Again, there's so many levels to being a quarterback and understanding an offense, and the more reps you get, the more comfortable you become with that. Um but again, I played a lot of football, so I think that my brain just kind of works a little bit different as a quarterback, so uh again, just going in, you know, day in day out, trying to get 1% better and that's kind of been the mindset. >> I know you're in [clears throat] shorts and you can't get hit and all that, but how much faster is this game than college? Can you put that in perspective? >> I mean, it's 100% faster. I mean, think like the the best guys from each college team are now all, you know, accumulated into one space, one not one team, but 32 different teams, right? And I obviously I speak for this team cuz it's the only defense I've gone against, but yeah, every I mean, everything just happens a tick faster and I think that a huge part of that is just the the mental side of it because as I got more comfortable with the offense, with the guys I was throwing to, building that chemistry over such a short period of time, obviously. And again, we're not in pads, I'm not getting hit, so it is different because the game speed, I mean, it it's something totally different than when you're in practice, but the game is still fast, especially if you have intention, which I feel like we have in practice and we get really good competes out there from the ones all the way down. It It was I thought it was a really good competitive I mean, from rookie mini camps OTAs to, you know, mandatory mini camp, it was really competitive and the guys were really flying around out there and we got really good work, but again, it's definitely faster and I feel like the you become in it. >> I know you'd like to, ideally, kind of ease into this a little bit, you know, and everything. It's just the beginning of your pro career, but you know, what appears to be there's a starting opportunity. Do you Do you try to speed up your process just knowing that there's opportunity right away maybe here? >> I mean, from day one, I mean, there was for me like I didn't want to ease into anything, you know, to be completely honest. I mean, shoot, again, from Monday through Friday, I mean, they wouldn't I mean, the rookies are are have to be here on Fridays, but I mean, I'm here 13 hours a day, you know, and I get in here early in the morning and obviously we have our stuff that's required and mandatory and I mean, I guess not necessarily mandatory, but obviously as a rookie you're going to be here and you're going to do it. And And then we we get done with practice and then we have our little rookie meetings and then I'm here, you know, up here with Coach Hackett, Coach Shob, ask Coach LaFleur a question if I had have something, but really just spending as much time with them. And I think it's really cool cuz obviously Coach Shob did it. He's he's been in the league. He he played he played the position, which so many it's so hard to understand what the position of quarterback is if you haven't actually done it, right? And he he has done it. He's he's been there. He's done it. Coach Hackett has coached amazing quarterbacks. Just such a smart mind. Coach LaFleur has coached amazing quarterbacks. Such a smart mind. So just trying to pick their brains and just take every little inch and every little thing to add it to my repertoire and get as, you know, good and as comfortable as I can is is something that I've done from the second I feel like I've stepped in the building. >> Outside of the mentally understanding the playbook, what's been the biggest adjustment physically for you in your game these last few weeks into this style? >> Yeah, I don't know if there really has been a physical adjustment. I feel like the really a lot of it is is the mental side. And the more comfortable you become and the more reps you get, I mean the the physical kind of just takes care of itself. You know, I've I've thrown thousands of footballs in my life. I've thrown thousands of dig routes, thousands of out routes, thousands of go routes. Now it's just combining that with timing, with chemistry, with understanding. And again, that's everything that comes with playing the position. So >> Snap count and being under center, are those easy adjustments for you being so different from college? >> I'd say different from last year at Miami. We didn't go under center a lot and obviously you really have like one or two snap counts. I think it's something that's really cool. Just how you can keep the defense off balance and then at Georgia I was under center a lot more than I was I was at Miami. So I have had reps at it in the past and now just again, the more reps you get now, the more comfortable you become with it, but it's not something that um has been foreign to me. >> You mentioned that you and the door that you have to figure out ways to kind of like keep diving into the playbook for 5 years. What kind of tactics can you take from that experience that you can use now in the NFL? >> Yeah, I think the biggest thing and something that I feel like it's looked over a lot, especially as a quarterback, um and and I kind of said it earlier is like doing the simple things like in an elite way. Like how elite can you be at the easy things? Cuz it again, the the flat route that gets you 7 yards on first down. I mean, it's not it's not sexy. It doesn't It's not the 45-yard go ball, right? Um that everybody wants to see, but it wins you football games. And um the more that you can commit to that, it it creates consistency and consistency wins football games. >> When you're out there and you're you're practicing, you're trying to learn the mental side, learn the physical side, just do what you need to do to become a better player. How does How does building chemistry work with pass catchers, the receivers, especially when, you know, you might not be getting reps with all of the different ones? Like how how does that How does that develop? >> So yeah, that's that's obviously the balance of all of this and trying to establish yourself as a a leader, but first you have to build connections to, you know, be able to establish yourself as a leader. So, um obviously, I think the biggest thing in that is how much time can I spend on my own, right? In my own time of getting in the playbook, making sure I understand and can actually go out there and do it. So, I'm not out there on the field like in just a a whirlwind of oh, like this guy's doing this, this guy's doing this. It's like no, I go up to the line and I feel comfortable and now I can focus on building that chemistry. Now I can focus on building those relationships. So, I feel like I mean, there's only so much time in the day, but um how much of that time can I allot to making sure that I'm becoming a a better quarterback, a better football player, a better teammate. >> If you look at purely at the order of reps during these spring practices, it seems like the veterans have been ahead of you so far. You know, that don't tell the full story. It doesn't necessarily mean much right now. But do you kind of feel like where you're where you kind of expected and wanted to be kind of at the end of mini camp? >> Yeah, I mean, for myself, I feel like I have very high expectations and I always have. I mean, my entire life. Um it's really, you know, what motivates me and I've always been very internally motivated. But for me, the biggest thing was coming in here, A, learning the playbook, B, building connections with my teammates, and then C, trying to become the best quarterback that I possibly can. And that's each and every day just trying to be better than the day before. Uh so for me, the expectations that I have for myself, I feel like I've been pushing those and pushing those and pushing those. And each day, I mean, they only get greater and greater because if if I was better than the day before, then okay, I need to be better the next day as well. And that's kind of just how I've always been wired. Um and and that's, you know, how I'll continue to approach it. >> What if you could If your yourself from 6 weeks ago is kind of saw where you are right now and where you feel like your game is at, is there anything that you you would be surprised by and kind of things that you've learned or or developed with yourself? >> Yeah, I mean, I kind of spoke on this um earlier. It's just the game is different. It just is. Um the the game is different. Just the way you know, things are called to the way that you read the defense to again, it it's more disguised. It's it's not you walk up to the ball and you kind of know what the defense is doing. You know where the ball's going to go pre-snap. So really honestly, I I kind of like it cuz it just it allows you to go out there and just react. Uh obviously, you you have a plan pre-snap of what you want to do. But at the end of the day, you just go out there, be an athlete and react, which I think makes it a little bit easier um at times cuz if it's not there, boom, check it down. You you got to I mean, shoot. We we got a bunch of backs, you know, get it down All right, they're going to make plays. Uh but again, it it's definitely different from you know, again, I I spoke on all of it. The speed, the the plays, the concepts, right? How you're you know, progressing through things, but I think it's been really cool. Uh just getting to learn the mental side and then obviously go out there and do it. >> What was it like spending a few few days with Jacoby and did your uh with both of you being from Florida, did that kind of help kind of ease any relationship, friendship, anything like that? >> Uh yeah, obviously um we got to spend a couple of days together uh during the mandatory mini camp. Um again, I I didn't get to talk to him much, but again, he seems like a great guy. Uh sat down, had a couple conversations, nothing obviously like super deep. I mean, we're we're in the facility, we're talking about football. So, again, he seems like a great guy and I'm excited to you know, continue to build our relationship. >> One of the things you had mentioned is demanding the huddle. How much of that is just the building on the relationships that you were talking about because sure as a rookie, it's different when you walk into a huddle and there's totally new faces and a lot of veterans. So, what kind of goes into demanding that huddle? >> I think the biggest thing is a performing and earning the trust of the people around you. Um it's hard to lead anything or demand anything if you're not out there, you know, performing and then the guys in the huddle don't trust you, right? You You got to step in the huddle with confidence and you got to be able to look at them and them look back at you and them know and have confidence that you're going to go out there and have success, right? And I think that's the biggest thing. So, continuing to go out there, perform, make plays, make the right plays, I think is important especially in you know, earning trust and establishing yourself as a leader. >> What was the evaluation of Jeremiah's arm at the D-backs game? >> Say that again? >> What was the evaluation for Jeremiah Love's arm at the D-backs game? >> I thought it was it was pretty good, you know, it didn't look the best, but I you know, he did throw a strike, which is important. I'm I'm surprised or I don't even know, do they normally make them scoot up a little bit, you know? They do. They always They don't let you throw it from the mound. I don't know. They might have They might have to make an exception to let me throw it from the mound if I ever do one. But, no, he I thought it was great. Yeah, threw a strike, so that's that's what we want. >> Carson, I'm curious if there's anything outside of being a quarterback that helped you develop your leadership skills, anything in life or family dynamics that helped you kind of mold yourself into the leader you are today? >> Hmm. That's such a good question. Um I'd say a huge part of it. So, my dad played linebacker at the Naval Academy, and I think that just that discipline of, you know, what it takes to be in the military or be in the Navy, and just that mindset that you have to have and being raised, you know, that way I think really helped me. And again, I played quarterback my whole life, so it kind of comes It doesn't kind of come with the position. It comes with the position. And when you're again, when you're in that huddle, everyone's looking at you. So, and I feel like for me, I've always wanted to, you know, take that step and want to be the guy that goes and makes the play. Want to be the guy that everybody, you know, looks on and and depends on. So, for me, again, I I think just from a young age, it was kind of just an innate ability thing. And I definitely accredit a lot of that to my dad. >> Any lessons you could share from Coach Shaw that clicked with you or resonated with you? I mean, you said you've been playing the position for so long for somebody that also did it, especially at this level. Anything stand out from your limited experience so far? >> I think there's so much. But, I think the biggest probably thing, and I think there's so many more experiences to learn from, but there's just one day after practice we're up there, and we're kind of just watching through like some of his two-minute drives. I think we had had like a two-minute period in in practice that day. And so, we went up and watched a couple of his two-minute drives from back in the day. And just watching him, you know, go do it and, you know, beat all these, you know, really, really good defenses, really good teams and go down there and win games. Um I thought it was pretty cool, you know, I just just watching him, you know, get to do it and watching the film. I mean, it was really grainy, you know, it was a long time ago. No, I'm I'm just kidding. I'm just kidding. I'm just kidding. Uh we always like to we always like to joke with him about that, but uh Nah, I I there's plenty more experiences to learn about that. But that was that was a cool moment for me to just sit down and you know, what go watch his games in the past and watch him uh do that and kind of, you know, teach on his experiences. >> You'll probably get a lot of reps in the Hall of Fame game. Have you and that's what, 2 weeks into camp, 3 weeks or whatever it is. Is that something you'll you'll think about during kind of the break? Is that something that you need to prepare for? >> Oh, absolutely. Uh 100%. I mean, it's already on my mind right now. Um Yeah, the the the break, you know, it's it's not much of a break. Um obviously we'll be working and I mean, I can speak for myself, but I think the the other guys understand that, too, of you know, the the mission and, you know, the mission that we're on and uh especially for myself, you know, making sure that I'm prepared and ready uh for those moments and that's what I'll do. >> What kind of opportunity can it be for you to get that that many reps in front of our >> Uh I mean, obviously it's a amazing opportunity, right? To not only, you know, showcase uh my skill set and what I can do, but for I mean, our entire team, you know, as we step into that game and the rest of the preseason.

title: New Details of Ravens Open Training Camp Practices | Ravens Final Drive
text: Training camp is right around the corner and today the Ravens announced new details around this year's camp schedule and ticketing process. The Ravens will have 12 free open practices here at the Under Armour Performance Center this summer and we have the ability to host 2,000 fans here each day for those practices. Now those tickets are free and they will be available to fans beginning July 9th at 11:00 a.m. Now we do have some changes coming to camp this year so this is important. First of all, the ticketing process is different this year. Now every guest needs an individual ticket to attend. Tickets used to be distributed per car but now they're going to be distributed per person. So again, every guest in attendance >> [music] >> needs your own ticket. Now fans are going to be able to claim up to four tickets per transaction and again, those free tickets will be available starting July 9th. The other big change is that parking will now be offsite at the Metro Center at Owings Mills. We'll then have complimentary motor coach shuttles to bring guests here to the Under Armour Performance Center. The new parking process will allow us to have significantly more fans here on site who we can host each day at those practices. It will be an excellent environment full of energy every day here at practice and we'll have waves of shuttles to the facility from the Metro Center starting an hour and a half before practice each day and then running throughout the day. Now the Ravens first full team training camp practice is coming up Wednesday, July 29th. The final date for fans attending training camp is Monday, August 17th. So it's going to be an exciting summer and we can't wait for camp to get here and see the flock here at the facility bringing [music] energy to these practices. Again, set your calendar to claim those passes on July 9th. [music] You can also get more information on everything related to training camp by visiting baltimoreravens.com/trainingcamp. That's it for me. Thanks for watching. We'll see you again tomorrow.

Uh for me like becoming like a growing soccer fan and obviously they're the most historically legendary team. um especially playing in a stadium that everybody knows of, a team that everybody knows about, like it's going to be it's going to be pretty special. And I just want to see like just the atmosphere um when we get in there and you know, I want to like when we get to like do our walkthroughs and practice in there, just kind of just take it in cuz those are opportunities that you get a lot. So, you know, I'm really excited to to bring the teammates, you know, all of us can go experience it and then they can maybe find a love for and enjoy for soccer as well. How do you think your level of fame here compares to those guys where they're playing? Is there anything is it similar at all? >> I mean, you just saw a goalie, you know, if you want for in perspective, like you just saw a goalie that had what, 50,000 followers. Um, and he had a he had a great it was a zero. It was tied 00, but he had a great game. Now he's had like 13 million followers. So, like >> it's such a world like the the the sport of soccer is so worldwide. Everybody watches around the whole whole world. And I know we're growing. Um like even when I go to other countries like you know there's a lot of like everywhere I go like people know it's a blessing that people know who I who I am right >> but >> I still be like like dang like you guys don't even watch football like that but I know like fantasy football is growing so much everywhere. Like I was in Japan and you know the the Japanese people were like they don't even watch the sport but they just pulled up the fantasy on their phone. They were like I was like oh there you go. So but them like they're known across the globe. So, I mean that's that's the difference. >> When did it dawn on you? Was there a moment when you realized that the scale of that was just different than what y'all are doing? >> Yeah. I mean, yeah. I mean, even when I was in France, like, you know, the the people that worked um at the facility, like wherever Mbappé went, like they were just like like just in shock >> that he and they see him every day. >> And it's like it's it's something new for them every single time when they see him. So, I know everywhere he goes, um it's the same thing. and they got to like it's it's literally they're they're bigger than most most celebrities. Um well, they're bigger than really all celebrities in America. So, you know, it's kind of cool to see like that transition with them and how they handle it, how they go about it. Um and just how they represent themselves. >> Obviously, Tyler and Brian are two different running styles. It's kind of similar a little more to you. Do you feel like that you could kind of I'd say learn a little more from him, but obviously your styles are more similar? Yeah, I mean, you know, what Tyler brought, um, he he he was special in in his game and how he ran the football and how he exploited defenders and how he created space for himself. Like, and then Brian's the same way. Um, you know, they they're not too different. Like, you know, they they both have some similarities that, you know, they they both run through people um on the field. like I always just kind of just see and and advise like what they do, what they do different and how I can help Brian's game and his all-around game because he's very talented clearly and I can't wait to see what we can do together. But um even just with Tyler like Tyler continued to kept growing uh year by year and you just saw like the growth of his game and then I know like Brian he he's grown so much in the past three months that we four months that we've been here and it's it's been cool to be a part of John, I've heard when you start the offseason program, new regime, new scheme, you're learning, how much more comfortable, how rewarding does it feel now to get to this point with all the work you put in? >> Yeah, I mean, it feels great. Um, you know, just knowing the scheme now and and really starting to be comfortable with it. Um, you know, that's always the goal when there's a new coach and a new OC. And I think Tommy and Kevin and Coach Petri, all the all the guys, like they've been such a they did such a great job with us and learning the whole aspect of the offense and the pass game, the run game. So like for me, you know, now I'm not really thinking about anything anymore. I'm just going out there and lining up and just trying to go be special. >> At least for me, I don't know if you've seen that massive Lamin who is next to your stadium, next to the >> I actually did see that. Yeah, I saw social media. >> How how big is the impact of Lamal here in United States? >> Yeah, I mean it's great, man. Like you know, he's he's such a an amazing player, especially for how young he is. I played garbage time my freshman year and then having to play snaps that actually, you know, count to win the game. It was like, yeah, from from 2018 to like 2021, I hadn't touched the hadn't touched the field. And then what Corey said is that after you had a really good year that year and you had to choose whether you wanted to stay or leave, you had a handful of I guess offers even prior to hitting or I guess you said you were never actually in the portal, but there were others who kind of reached out. But so why did you want to stay? >> Um family, you know, I'm big on loyalty. Uh they invested in me so and nothing meant more to me than just being hearing my name called on draft day. Michael Jordan from the University of Finley. uh that meant more to me than going to another school and letting somebody else take credit for something that we built there. So that that meant the most to me. >> What Cory said too that kind of surprised me is you're the last division 2 player who's who's drafted and the way that >> everything in that world is changing. It might remain that way for a long time. I take pride in that. >> I do. I mean, I feel like, you know, I feel like, yeah, I do take pride in it. I mean, with how NIL is going and everything, man. Uh, yeah, it's a blessing to be the last so far in the last two years, the last division, too. It's like, it's crazy. I wish guys would stay cuz it's it's an honor to be coming from D2. It shows everybody you get out the mud. But, you know, can't, you know, just just take it for what it is. >> And then just out out here, I mean, how do you feel as a as a the one's right tackle, but if you're so far out here? >> Uh, I feel good. Um, I'm happy to, you know, continue to keep fighting for a job, earn trying to earn a job. Um, you know, it's a blessing to be here. Um, and a blessing to be in a position to where I can earn a job. So, >> how much do you think? >> Thank you. >> How much do you think all these reps, you know, this offseason have helped you develop? >> A lot. A lot. Definitely a lot. You know, the the best way to get better at football is by playing actual football. you mean going to the I mean I spend time in the gym and in the lab, you know, whatever people want to call it, working on technique, but you don't actually get to get better unless you're getting out here and you iron sharpens iron. So getting to getting to go up against, you know, our best players, you know, it's been helping me out and I've been able to use the things that I've learned this offseason into this OTAAS and um mentor mini camp. >> So what what has your uh your Falcons experience been like so far the last few months? >> I'll tell you it's really been something that I've truly enjoyed. It's an opportunity to really be at the forefront of building something. We've got great leadership here. Um, starting with Mr. Blank, Matt, coach, and it's just a a great opportunity to get on the ground floor of something that's being built and really excited about it. So, it's been two months. You know, it's been it was a hectic first probably 24 days or whatever it was leading up to the draft and then now really working to put into process um what we're trying to build going forward and really kind of focus in on our people and and what we can build. >> Eagles have been one of the you could say that they've been the premier franchise in the NFL for for several years. Is there is there a single thing that you can take from a winning organization and a and it's like apply it to every organization or is it just something that was intrinsic there and you're building something new here? >> I think um first I I'd say I'm very grateful for my time in Philadelphia. Uh learned from a lot of great people there. Um Howie Roseman taught me a lot and I really am grateful for that opportunity. Now, bringing it here, I'd say the number one thing that is something Ian preaches and it's something coach preaches is an a relentlessness as terms of team building. Things don't ever stop. It's something we constantly want to try to evolve and grow and continue to get better. And I think bringing that here, the guys who are in here all have the same similar mindset. And that's something for me going forward here that really is a calling card that will be a calling card of ours going forward. >> How did you wind up your leg? Like how did your your spring unfold a little bit? Like it kind of happened late, right? Like how did it go? >> Yeah. Um I was going through the normal offseason process um in Philadelphia and went through that preparing and just had the opportunity. I think it was early April, late March, you know, to be requested to come here and um thankfully was given the opportunity in Philly to come out and was happy to be here. Again, you know, the opportunity to get with Ian um get with Matt on the ground floor of of building something was something that was just too too good to pass up for me. from kind of a larger view of looking at the roster here, what impressed you when you arrived here? Like I mean, how do you view it? >> I mean, it's hard not to immediately see the talent that that's here. Um there there's a lot of talent already on the roster and one of the biggest things for us is to continue to build on to that talent to uh to I think Ian talked about raising the floor a lot and that's something that is our focus at this time and that comes with that relentlessness. There are a number of different ways to acquire players and we're always going to be on the look for opportunities to get better. But I mean, having the talent that was already here, I mean, that's a it's a great opportunity to build on and all of us kind of working together, getting with coach and and really going forward with his plan and just accentuating the guys that were already here. >> Did you cross path with first in Philly or did y'all go back any before that? >> Yeah. No, we we worked together for I believe about six months in Philadelphia. Yeah, I came in June or May or June. Um, and then he left in January uh to go to the Bears. So, we had a short crossover there. Uh, but continued to, you know, obviously you you meet people in this business and you develop relationships and we're like-minded. Ian believes in people and process and those are two things that I I truly think help build my career going forward is relationships and process. So, it's a good match. >> You got any good Steph stories? >> Any good Steph stories? I got a few of those from uh from back at Davidson. It was uh I was two years ahead of him. Um I laugh because probably I think of him differently than than the world does. Um, but it's amazing to see what he's done. Um, and it's even easier. It's actually funny. It's very, you know, it's great to root for great people. And I think that's some of the things that we have here. When you talk about the superstars here, they're really good people here. So, it makes it easy to root for. >> When you guys made the deal for for Wani Morris, what did you see in him specifically to make that? >> I think again, it's about raising the floor. you know, when when you have opportunities to improve the roster, you're always going to take those uh especially up front. Up front, we believe in building it up front and we're going to take a number of different swings and continue to try to build I think you guys went through that last year with kind of the injury bug up front and it's something that happens to every team all across the league. And uh when I was in Washington at one point, I want to say we had 16 or 17 different offensive line uh lineups over the season. It's a natural part of our of our game and you have to be prepared and that's what building that depth and you know building the bottom of the room is You >> did work with Bryce Johnson. Yes. in Philly about how impactful is he especially with the big deals that have been made obviously for Drake and then the ones on the >> Yeah, Bryce uh I had the office right next to Bryce. Bryce is an amazing um mind, good football mind, great person. Uh he thinks about things in in different ways and I think it's a it's a special skill. He gives us the you know someone there who can create that and and be a weapon in that space. But the reality again, he's a great person. It all kind of goes back to the people. Um, he understands what we're trying to do and is always going to kind of push that going forward. So, it makes it easy when you work with good people and you're always focused on the same thing. Everyone working in one accord. >> When you say amazing mind, like what is that? Like how how unique is his mind? >> I mean, Bryce is one of the smartest people I've been around. I can just put it to you like that. He's smart. He thinks about things in different ways. Um, and it really is an opportunity. I think you'll see through the things we do here. We will always, you know, protect the club, but make sure the players happy about what thing what things happen and come their way as well. >> Take us through your perspect deal. Does it help that he's done the previous deals for top of the line running backs that can help figure that situation out? >> I think, you know, one thing I'm not going to talk about kind of, you know, anything that may be theoretical or ongoing. Uh, that's just we're not going to negotiate kind of in the media, but I do appreciate the question. Taking it through your perspective a little bit when you're in these front office roles going from organization to organization, you know, what is the appeal and also challenge of leaving a place that's very established and had a lot of success and going to a place like you said, ground floor with a lot of newness and new alignment, you know, straight down from president of football as a head coach. >> Yeah. I I think everybody gets in this business because they like to build. It's it's something that you want to do. you want to have the opportunity to impact the decisions that are made. Um, and this was a really good opportunity with good people. Uh, there's talent here. It's a great organization. Um, it's a great city. Again, these are all opportunities. I don't think anything is negative about taking that step in your career. It's really just taking the next step and and trying to build and focus and grow. So again, I loved my time in Philadelphia. I enjoyed my time back in Washington. Uh great memories, great times, but now it's about, you know, going forward here with the Falcons. >> You guys had Jan Dawson and Philly now he's here. Uh what do you like about him and and you know what what is his role? What is the vision for him here? >> I think Jan Jan really has an opportunity here to you know to be kind of the player that he's always been. Um, obviously in in Philadelphia there are a lot of a lot of mouths to feed with the ball. Um, but I think again he works hard. He is consistent. He's a good person. These are all things again I think there's probably a common theme you guys will hear. That's what we're trying to build. And he's got a great opportunity as do a lot of our guys. I think competition is a real thing. Um, it's something we really are pushing here and going forward that's going to be our mantra. >> A lot of one-year deals on this team this year. Was that an intentional thing or what's the strategy with that? >> I think a lot of that was done actually before I got here. Um, so I I don't want to specifically comment on it, but it gives guys opportunity. I I think any of us in this room are really looking for opportunity. We're always looking for opportunity. So, when you have that many guys on one-year deals, it's opportunity for everyone. >> Do you think that that kind of influences the overall persona or or mental makeup of the team? >> I think naturally it does. I think, you know, again, guys want to be where they have a chance and they're all going to get their opportunity here. Um, one of the beautiful things about June is that we don't play next week. So, you don't have to worry about, you know, who's exactly suiting up. they'll have their opportunity to compete in camp and we're looking forward to it. >> Talk about what's unique with Matt Ryan as the head of this having been former player. Just from your perspective, what's that been? >> Yeah. Um I think you know it's easy to see very quickly. Uh Matt's awesome. He's smart. He's been there. The experience he has as a player, as a former player, and it's not just a former player. I mean, as an NFL MVP, uh, you don't get that kind of experience and kind of opportunity to sit down with somebody of that caliber and go through things. I think Ian talked about uh leading up to the draft when we were sitting down, we were watching wide receivers and Matt came in and he was able to give his perspective from being a you know a quarterback and what he's looking for and we talked about it from the front office perspective of what we were looking at. And that really was probably one of the coolest moments of my career to sit down and really get that kind of firsthand knowledge from someone who's pulled the trigger in the biggest games possible. >> Jeff, with Matt, um he always said at the start of this, you know, his job was to hire the GM, hire the coach, you know, do that and offer support wherever he can. You know, he done the first two. just how have you seen him make his imprint um you know sort of daytoday and where things have stood from even after those hires to where they are right now the Matt Ryan impact so to speak. >> Yeah, I mean Matt if when he said he's here to support in any way he really is. I mean you guys see out of practice he'll help with kind of anything. I know he's done like you know some scout team you know helping with the defense. He's in our meetings and helping with us, but I really think it's really wherever we need help. Um, he's willing to step in. He has no ego. He's always offering his, you know, his support of, hey, you can go talk to him. I'm thinking about this. He'll offer his support. If you ask for his opinion, he's going to give it. But I think to have somebody again of that caliber who is no ego and really is about the organization and helping people, it's amazing. I mean, that's we couldn't be any luckier to have him in that role. >> I know you see him on scout team every now and then, you know, doing whatever is necessary. Is there an example that you can point to, you know, that we obviously don't see behind closed doors in the front office? You said, "Wow, this is this is something that Matt really was impactful with." Well, I think you know just the the example of sitting down with him before the draft and again being able to watch players from his perspective again I don't think many front office front offices get the opportunity to sit down with a quarterback and again quarterback of that caliber and go through that process. And that for me was a first in my career and something that now that we've had I want to do it again. You know what I mean? There's always opportunity to learn and I don't think anybody has everything all figured out. But if we sit down and we have real discussions, real conversations, then we then we can get better as an organization. And I think at the end of the day, it's falcon decisions. It's not one person's decision. So time for one more. >> Can you talk about the difference of watching or seeing Bejon in Philadelphia from the perspective of Philadelphia and now being here and seeing him? Yeah, my perspective is the 24 week two um when they you guys came up there and and kind of ran all over us. I I think he's such a he's an exceptional talent. Um but again, he's a even better person. He makes it easy to root for. Uh I think there isn't, you know, he has the opportunity to kind of do what he wants. He's extremely skilled and that's something that we're lucky to have here. And I think it just continues to show every day. >> Is he the X factor for the team in terms of success here? >> I don't know that we would name a X factor, but is he a significant factor? Of course. Of course. >> Right. But a separator, you know, in in in close games or whatever. >> I think any of your good players have the opportunity to be the separator at any different point. Different games turn out different ways uh depend on how things unfold. and he absolutely has the opportunity to be one of those on our team. >> Parkley said nobody cuts like him. Do you agree? >> I love Saquon. Seaquan is is a great guy, but you know, I'm I'm focused on the Falgas at this point. Thank you.

title: Tua Tagovailoa on Atlanta Falcons mandatory minicamp and building camaraderie on and off field
text: It's hot in Miami, it's hot here, which is hotter? >> Oh, Miami for sure. >> Okay, I mean >> Miami, no doubt. >> not being landlocked if it would be different, but yeah, interesting. >> Yeah, I mean it it it's not to say that it's not hot. It is hot, but uh yeah, Miami, it's that air is thick out there. >> Mhm. >> Today was really nice. >> Today was amazing. >> Today was nice. >> Uh Tua, how would you just kind of uh encapsulate everything that's happened not just during this mini camp, but over the last month or so? >> I think it's been really good to be able to build relationships with guys um not just within the quarterback room, but guys in in other rooms and then be able to sort of cross the line onto the defensive side and get into know those guys a little bit better and guys that I've played against over my my years with Miami. Pick their brains a little bit and I think it's been been a really cool transition. It's been really smooth and I think this is one of the best locker rooms I've I've been a part of. >> What makes that Why so? >> The human beings that we got in there. Their faith. Sort of the talk that we have. Not a lot of small talk. We're going to talk about football for sure. We're in we're in a locker room, but outside of that just guys talking about their families what their families mean to them and what football is able to provide for them throughout you know, whatever their their family's going through in that initial moment being here being able to be here, get away and being able to uh sort of look back and think when I was 10 years old, this is what I've always wanted to do. Now that I have a family you know, things kind of change, but I'm still able to live out my dream being able to take care of them. So, I think that's what makes this locker room so unique. >> I wonder if you feel like the competition has really at quarterback has really started yet given that Michael is not full go or do you feel like it sort of starts when training camp is? >> I think competition is is going to be there whether it is said or whether it's not said. This is the NFL. You're either coming out there to compete or you're not. You know, I think we we've all been in this league for for some time to know this isn't something that you can you can walk through. Um you know, this is something that uh whether it's in a meeting room, uh you know, we we we all got to take our job serious in whatever capacity we can do it to. And so I I look at at it all as a competition, but um needless to say that I don't think that changes my relationship with anyone, you know, on the team. Mike, um Trevor Kyle Pitts, whether I'm the guy, whether I'm not the guy, you know, I'm I'm I'm here to help in whatever way that is. >> Tua, what can you say about the wide receiver room, especially Zach Kittle Branch? You mentioned his speed and that being kind of comparable to some receivers when you were at Miami. >> Yeah, I mean, we we have we have a lot of dudes um and a lot of the guys in that receiver room, it it's tall, it's medium tall, if you will, it's short, it's fast, it's not too fast. Uh you you have a variety of of of receivers and you also have a variety of pass catchers within the tight end room. So you just got to be able to build a relationship, build that chemistry with those guys throughout OTAs, routes on air, and then team periods, what guys run certain routes best. Uh you kind of put that into a box and you you can kind of gauge, all right, this is the route we we would like for this guy to run versus, you know, another guy. We he'd probably be better on this route. >> Do you feel like you've been spoiled from time at Alabama, Miami, and to now with all the receivers that you have? >> Oh, for sure. I I wouldn't say spoiled. I've I've been very blessed, man. Uh to be able to throw to some really good wide receivers, some really good pass catchers. >> What are your impressions of Kevin Stefanski so far? >> He says what he means and he means what he says what he says. Um you know, a lot of a lot of uh things that I've heard within team meetings, within after practice meetings is the little things matter. It's all about the little details with him. >> He doesn't strike us at least as a guy who raises his voice much or repeats himself much. Is that the way he is? >> Yeah, I I I wouldn't say he's a guy that raises his voice much. Um it's just a guy who what you see is what you get. Um but when he does speak, uh it kind of it kind of has some weight behind it. >> Is there anything quarterbacking wise that he or Alex Van Pelt or any of these guys have told you that was new to you? I mean, you've been doing this a while. You've had a ton of coaches. Is there any nugget that they've dropped you know, that's fresh? >> Uh I I would say nothing fresh. Uh but I would say the biggest thing that they harp on is is playing within the rhythm, the timing of your footwork. So, making sure your feet feet are right. So. >> Kevin said you've seen some old school cutups in in practice going back to like AVP's days. >> What's the what's the furthest back you've seen them hit him pull up a cutup? >> I don't know. It's pretty far back >> [laughter] >> It's pretty far back there. I don't want to get the years wrong. >> Is it Is it surprising to you that some of those old cutups are still kind of relevant to modern quarterback play? >> You know, not necessarily. I would say there's been changes within defenses, within offensive schemes, uh within the way the quarterbacks would drop from under center and how the quarterback position has evolved from under center to more into the gun. Um but you got to have a base. You got to have a foundation of what football is. And so, I think it's always good to to go and watch games way back when um you know, how guys would play the the type of toughness you needed to have to play in in a league like that uh back in those times. Uh so, uh I I I think you can you can gather some really good good information and some really good things by just watching players. Mhm. >> Have you had a chance to sit down with Matt Ryan and what are you kind of looking to learn from him? >> I haven't had a had a chance to sit down with Matt. Uh we've been we've been buzzing here with installs with talking to to to the guys in in their respective rooms. So, it it's been it's been pretty tough. We just been trying to dial in on making sure everyone knows where to go, knows where to be, uh and then the timing aspect of of the offense, too. >> You said a minute ago that, you know, competition's everywhere, but you're here to help the team no matter what. How tough How tough is that when it's sort of the unknown of your competitor, you want to be the guy, you want to play, and then also knowing that there might be, you know, that opportunity might not be there, that it might be someone else playing quarterback. How do you balance the competition of what you want to do with helping the team when you're not on the field? >> You know, I don't think it's as tough as uh people would would want me to say it it's it's tough. I'm a competitor, don't get me wrong. But I'm also a believer, too. And um you know, I believe if it's God's plan for me to to play here, not to play here, I'm okay with it. There's there's nothing There's nothing wrong with that. I believe there's a greater purpose than this being a game. I don't know if you heard what I just said, but it's just a game that we're able to play and we're able to take care of our families through this game. And I've been so so freaking blessed, so fortunate, um you know, to be able to to have this opportunity and you know, to have been blessed with the gifts that I have. >> I mean, Kevin said it earlier, it's June. So, the beauty of June is you don't have to go out and play that there's a lot of time to it. It's 41 days from now until the start of training camp. Uh to get to that point, what's the biggest thing that you want to improve I don't want to say improve on, but that you want to you know, make sure you're fine-tuned with before you get out there that you feel that you're game ready by the time, you know, that rolls around. >> Yeah, I I would say just continuing to lock in with the playbook. Uh it it's new not just to me, but to to a lot of the guys uh that were here last year and years prior. So, just lock into that and then, you know, see what Mike's doing and then see what everyone else is doing in terms of wanting to throw and and whatnot with what their vacation plans are. >> It's early on, what are you kind of looking forward to in this offense? >> Sorry. >> It's early on, but what are you kind of >> Well, I I I like that we push the ball down the field. Uh we push the ball down the field a good chunk and um you know, I I like how we're we're trying to mirror our our pass game with our run game, so. >> Anything else? >> Yeah, one more just fun little bit. Are you into the World Cup at all? Watching any any of it? >> I I don't watch any of it. Sorry. I mean, I'm I'm not going to lie about it. I Sorry. Yeah. >> That's all good. >> You're a little busy right now. >> And why have you BS through it? >> No, yeah, yeah. >> All good. >> I Thanks, guys. Appreciate it. Oh, yeah, yeah. Go ahead, brother. >> You speak about faith a lot. He's a big believer. You had a chance to connect with him and what are some of those conversations that you do partake? >> Yeah, I've I've had um a fair amount of conversations with him about it. I would say the first time that I signed here, uh he was the first person to text me. And I thought that was really really cool. You know, he's he's a star in this league. And he's been so for for the time that he's entered the league. But we've shared some stuff. You know, I'd probably like to keep a lot of it private, but just know that we have we have talked about it. Mhm.

title: Atlanta Falcons Head Coach Kevin Stefanski discusses Mandatory Minicamp & player strengths
text: Heat. Heat. [music] >> [music] >> Hey hey hey. Hey, hey, hey. >> Hey, hey, uh saw that that Drake didn't practice yesterday. Uh any injury insight [clears throat] on on what's going on? >> Yeah, a little thing that I'm just being ultra cautious. He could practice, but I'm holding him out. >> And kind of same question about Xavier Watts. >> Very similar. >> Well, had a really strong year last year. Where's that next step? Is that in your opinion? >> Very naturally, the the freshman to sophomore year transition. And I think we've talked about this before. It just you you you bring the experience of that lap around the sun with you and it allows you to be better in really all aspects of your professional life. Meaning uh it your routine you've established uh the schematics you've you've done before. So uh it it brings some confidence in into your play. Uh so Xavier, like all of our guys going into year two, uh you you lean on the experiences of year one, uh to to then take a leap, uh if you will. >> One thing that that Hood mentioned to me a few weeks ago is that Xavier and Jesse have this like unspoken bond back there where they can see things and they're aligned with how they see it and they don't even have to say it. How unique is that? How much can that help you guys? That's extremely important to have that and especially when you have that you can have versatility to what you're doing with both players and uh the good news is those are two extremely intelligent players and like you like Hood mentioned like like you mentioned just their relationship and and how they can feed off of each other and a lot of the dialogue and the communication that happens back there oftent times is signal or or sometimes non-verbal uh communicating amongst yourselves out to the corners certainly with the linebackers uh in the nerve center But having guys that uh are on the same page is a very big deal. And and when you have that, then you can push the envelope a little bit in terms of scheme and asking to do a little bit more. And uh you know, we may ask this safety to drop down in the box and then this one to go to the post, but if we get this look, we're going to change it or you're both going to be back. And there's just no end to what you can do uh when it comes to X's and O's. But you have to have the players that are capable of of doing all that. And we have that with our safeties. What are your impressions of Brian Nel? >> Uh, you know, pros pro. Uh, very impressed with news, how he approaches his craft. Uh, just a a guy that's always here, it seems. Um, even before the offseason program began, just always here and working. Uh, those centers, the intelligence that you have to have to keep everybody on the same page, to orchestrate the run game, to orchestrate the pass protection game. I've been very blessed to be around some very intelligent centers and and I think news is right there with those guys. >> For what you want to do, do you have a a physical type for that position? Would you lean toward more athletic? Would you lean towards stout? >> Yeah, I I think with all of our positions, certainly there's things that you're looking for, but you can't be so stringent in those and miss out on good players. So, they come in all shapes and sizes. I've been around some really tall guys, some shorter guys, some guys that are wide and and sturdier and bulkier, if you will, guys that can move. I I just think it's really take a really good player and then it's our job as as coaches to uh find out what they can do and lean into those uh strengths of theirs. >> We were talking to ADP and we talked to you a little bit about this as well, just the footwork as far as the quarterbacks go and how important that is and how much you guys are underscoring that. Why is that? Why is that so important and how much have you done that in other places as well? >> I think we're all disciples uh of Bill Walsh and and you know how you play this game is is from the ground up and uh you know I've been around some great offensive coaches. Gary Kubak comes to mind and somebody that talked about you know listening to your feet and our feet are our clock. You don't have a stopwatch back there when you're playing quarterback but you do have your feet. So a fivestep drop in a hitch is timing. So, if the ball has to come out on five plant uh because it's this many steps by the receiver, that that's the precision that's required in the passing game. If it's a sevenst step drop with a hitch, it that's the precision based on the depth of the route by by the uh that's a fine uh based on the on the depth of the route of the receiver. So, there's so much that goes into precision in the passing game, but it starts with timing, and timing only comes from the the footwork of the quarterback. Would you say it's more what you guys doing is more kind of reinforcing what those guys already know or are you adding different wrinkles to >> I I think every team what I just described every single team in the NFL does it versions of this and certain routes have certain drops that are are matched up with it and not all drops are created equal. So a fivestep drop for this route may be a little bit different for this route because we could talk about stretching those five a bit. So it's no different. It's just hanging your head on what you believe but it's something that we believe and it's something that we preach. something that we teach and it's certainly something the guys understand is important to playing that position. >> Did you do you have a copy of or have read Bill Walsh that finding the winning edge book? >> I do. I have a copy and AVP shows the guys he has some install tapes of coach Walsh back in the day of of installing some plays and and it's it holds up. You know, it's it's football's football and and getting to see some of the you know the the great ones do the same drills that we're doing and AVP played for Paul Hackett when he was at pit. Uh so it's an AVP breaks out the tape of of his uh college days. Often there's some receivers in three-point stances that we're not employing, but >> [laughter] >> um but it's it's it's a good message to our guys when you have a teacher, in this case, Coach Vampelt, showing them this is how I was taught.
