You know, uh, there's more extreme circumstances in the pre- snap in terms of what you need to communicate. Um, so those guys embrace it. you know, there are certain people who are giving communication, there are certain people receiving it by position, not necessarily by their personality. Um, we don't really care about that. Like, if you're in a position of communication and you're commanding and you're responsible for the checks and things we have to do, that's what you have to do. So, whether you say a thousand words out of these walls or two, it doesn't matter. When we're on that grass, it's it's a premium. >> Did you talk to guys who were here last year about the breakdowns communication wise to help you say, "Okay, this messed up last year. we're going to make sure we >> I didn't that had nothing to do with me. So, I was more so focused on how we were going to move forward. Um, and just making sure that we had the the right mindset and approach in terms of what we believe in on how we want to play >> Christian Todd Archer with ESPN. What's it been like to go from you've had your position groups and then to go in front of the entire defense to have to communicate with the entire group? Is that something you had done either previously in Denver or Philly? >> Yeah, I've done that before. Obviously, not at this rate. I think the the thing that's most different is like, you know, we start off, we have an hour block and, you know, we'll start with the unit, I'll go, they break up to position meetings. It's like, well, where do I go now? Um, and then in practice, during individual, I'm used to getting my hands dirty and then I'm, you know, walking around with my arms crossed like I'm a security guard or something. So, I try to figure out how to keep myself occupied during those moments. So, it's been good, good transition, popping in and out of rooms and doing those things. And sometimes I'll, you know, meet with only the back seven, adjust the front seven after we finish that unit meeting. But um it's been a good adjustment. >> Do you try and because you have the DB background? Do you try to stay away from them because you know that one and try to go to the other groups more to or do you >> I do. There's still like we break stretch there's like this magnetic pull that like pulls me to the direction of the DBs. Luckily they switch where they start individually so I can't naturally find them every single time. So I try my best to stay away from that. Um, you know, I I still go over there, um, still talk to those guys, communicate with them, but, um, at the end of the day, it's about, you know, all levels, and I I try to make sure I I do that at a at a high level. >> John Micho at the Athletic, what have these last four or five months been like for you, uh, in here, away from here, getting settled in here, uh, going from, you know, position to being DC. What have it been like for you? >> Uh, it's been good. I mean, it's been, obviously, it's a lot. It's an increase in responsibility. It's an increase in um even my communication. Um Calvin asked about that like just what what I'm responsible for communicating to the staff, coaching them like they're my position group. Um and then just getting used to the area, you know, I walk back and forth. I'm still in the hotel, so I walk back and forth, so that's that's easy. I don't have to deal with traffic. Um but everything else just in terms of the increased responsibility, I think is um it was to be expected. So, you know, the new things they you know, they're going to happen. So, you just got to be prepared for things out of your control. But um I think that we have a great staff. I think Shotti's been great with his communication style. Um Will Mcclelay and the Joneses when we were going through the draft process. So everything has been great in terms of the communication and very clear expectations of of what I need to do and what the staff needs to do. >> Uh speaking of expectations, just has Caleb DS met those expectations that you had before the draft and just kind of where is that working relationship at right now? >> Yeah, he has. I mean he's he's as advertised. We we spent significant time with him before the draft process. we had a good feel on who he was and um knew some people at Ohio State, at Alabama um in terms of how he was on the dayto-day that we maybe didn't see in that 30 visit or or at the combine. Um but he's been doing great. He's a worker. You know, he he looks for coaching. He you know, he he craves that. He wants to be corrected. He wants more information. Um and he works as hard as he can with the extras and everything else. So, um it's it's been good. He's been good to work with. And I think that he's trying to um advance at the right rate. You know, I think that um we try to lessen those expectations in terms of what goes on outside of these walls. There's a certain process to take as a as a rookie in general in the National Football League and we try to abide by that process. >> Tommy, >> Tommy Y, Dallas Cowboys.com. As you've gotten to know your players and watch them in practice as you bounce around to different places, who's stood out to you in leadership roles early on here? >> Yeah, I think you you know, everything starts up front. So, I would say, you know, with with Quinnon and and Kenny, um Rashan coming in, you know, those guys have taken a significant step forward in terms of um just the uh pro habits. You know, those guys have rookies in their rooms, but they in affect the whole defense. Um those guys have really taken the bull by the horns in terms of um how we practice, you know, the strain and effort it takes and just leading by example. Their habits in the meeting room, pre-practice, postpractice, those guys are true professionals. Um so, I would say it starts with them. And then CD said a couple weeks ago that it was annoying to go against your defense in practice and some of the looks that you present. Have you had the inverse of that where you go up against Brian's offense and it's like ah this is it's kind of tough. >> Yeah, I mean I I think you want that. You want to be strained um in the offseason. You know we're not game planning against each other so everything is you know unscouted, unscripted look sometimes and um you know you don't want to we don't want to put um training wheels on anything. You know we want to go head first into it. So the more exposure we get to the jet motions and formation shifts, route concepts, run concepts that are going to challenge us in terms of our structure and our rules, you know, we welcome that. So it's been a it's been a good offseason for it. >> Nick Harris, forward Telegram, you can assemble your staff and have an idea of what it looks like, but actually seeing them on the grass and seeing them coach, what have you come away with from from your staff? >> Yeah, I think we we we got it right. You know, those guys are all um they're they're incredible teachers. Um they come with great energy. They're great teammates to work with. um they've really uh owned the responsibility of being the head coach of their position group um and supporting me in that process. So um I couldn't be happier with the with the staff that we've put together here. >> It might be too early for this question, but has there been any trial and error from your standpoint, whether it's building the scheme or how you structure your practice or anything that you've done and you're like, "Yeah, I'm not going to do the same next time." >> Uh yeah, I think that's every offseason though. I think um every offseason, this is what the offseason is for. There's going to be certain things you put out there that, you know, things sound good in the air conditioning. You know, it's 68, 70°, it's controlled. You get out there, it ain't 70° out there. I promise you that. So, um, you know, that that's part of the process. And some things you work through, you fix the rules, you tweak, and some things you're like, well, this probably isn't for us. Um, but you have to get that exposure for it. Sometimes it's from a schematic perspective, sometimes it's about personnel. So, um, or maybe it's just the phase that we're in right now with everything else that we're doing. So, um, no, that's been a good process to have because you you learn from those moments as well. >> Garrett Podell, CBS Sports. Christian, players have said your actual play calls are only handful of words. What goes into that and how can just a few words communicate everything that you're trying to get across for them on a given play? >> Yeah. Um, it's a long process because there's like, um, there are different word banks, you know. So, there's an Excel document that lives on my desktop. I mean, you know, you got weapons, NBA teams, um, insects, whatever, you know, and it's like, well, do we have enough inventory here that's going to fit this type of scheme, or do we have enough SNW words or FNB words or um, whatever it might be. Um, so it takes a lot to go into that. We try to be intentional with that in terms of those words having meaning, certain letters having meaning. Um, and just you don't want to have, you know, five, six word play calls when teams are going fast and guys have to communicate that in the huddle and outside of it. So, being able to condense that and have those things being very direct, um, is a good process to go through and I think our guys have embraced it. >> And how valuable is it giving your defenders that extra time before play to analyze the offense and diagnose it versus trying to figure out where everyone's supposed to? >> Oh, it's very important. I mean, because there's so many things from when the linebacker or the safety or whoever has the green dot is communicating that you break the huddle, what's the situation? Offense breaks the huddle, what personnel group are they in, what's the formation, um where is a certain player that we might be doing a double team to or whatever the case might be. Like, there's so many things to process from the play call to the snap. So, the best that I can shorten that process for them by being very direct and making sure that we get constant reps at that, then I'll try to put it on my plate, not theirs. >> Joe White, Dallas Morning News. One thing Jerry Jones talked about when they hired you is how much of a teacher you are. Some of the players have talked about pop quizzes and exams that you guys have had. Uh how where does your teaching philosophy come from and how much pride you take in that? >> Uh I take a lot of pride in it. I think our staff takes a lot of pride in it as well at the um at the foundation of if if you're a coach, you're a teacher. That's the essence of what we do. Um we have to get guys taught schematically, technically, fundamentally, all those things and and allow them to come to life. So, um, you know, I think just over the years, you kind of have different ways of doing it, whether it's cahoots, whether it's, you know, hard quizzes, whether you give guys a personal whiteboard to carry around in a meeting room, whether you put them on the board in your office and surprise them, whether it's film and have them write out responses and hand it back to you. Like, there's so many different ways to check for understanding and that's all we're trying to do. Again, that goes back to the communication and making sure that everybody's on the same page. Um, you don't want guys sit there in silence and assume that anybody knows anything. So, it's a constant process of getting those mental reps. um you know, you're kind of tricking your brain into thinking it's another rep on the field when you're, you know, doing it on the paper. So, we try to take that approach and just be as thorough as possible. >> Tim Call, Dallas Morning News. Uh two years ago, the challenge was to get Cooper Dean and Mitchell up to speed real quickly and obviously it went as good as it can go. Do you see this challenge similar to that? Not necessarily all with rookies, but downs and a couple, but with with different position groups on this defense getting them very quickly to where they need to get compared to where they were a year ago. >> Um, well, first thing I used to watch you on around the horn, so um, >> yeah. U, but no, I think that, um, yeah, it's it's different by position. There's certain things that we can't do with the front right now because we don't have pads on. Um, there are certain things the secondary can't do because they don't have pads on. I think that right now it's about the NFL 101. You know, what is the league? What family do these play callers come from? What do certain formations mean? Where's your help? Where isn't your help? Um who are you working with and communicating with? Do you know who you're looking at when you're talking or trying to hear something? Just getting those foundational things now. Um and not trying to, you know, walk before we crawl in in that essence. So, um we're in that process. We're kneede in it. Um, and you know, there's really no way to predict when that light is going to truly come on because, you know, we have plenty of time before the first game um, in New Jersey. So, we're just trying to follow those steps um, and have some urgency in doing it. Kind of throw them in the fire a little bit um, and just kind of see how they respond. >> And my second question has nothing to do with how you started your answer, but are you comfortable with uh, the title defensive coordinator franchise savior? Um the first one, yes, cuz that's what I do. Um the second one, uh no. You know, because it's about the collective and I think that we're all uh just as equally responsible for that. Um for the good and the bad. So, I'm just trying to do my part. >> Babe, Babe Laugh, Cowboys Radio Network and also used to watch Tim Kashaw on Around the War. We have something in common. >> Um so, Kristen, how how much of your time is now devoted to coaching the coaches? And I know you've got experience with a couple of them, but you know, you're coaching the coaches as well on trying to get the players together and that's constantly evolving, but how much of your time has been focused getting them up to speed as to what you want to >> um Yeah, a lot. You know, I would say, um, it starts in our defensive staff meeting room. Um, you know, that's where it starts. That's our field in a sense in terms of our communication. What does the film look like? What do we expect? What do we want it to look like? It's a very collaborative process as well. Um, and it doesn't start, you know, stopping these walls. You know, I've gotten text messages from Ryan Smith at 11:00 p.m. Um, you know, it's a constant communication. There might be one thing that we see just to check for that confirmation and to make sure that everybody's on the same page. So, uh, we try to spend that time and try to make sure that we have a collaborative approach so everybody's voice is being heard and we can get to a final result together, you know, so when we leave that room, then we have a united front. >> Sydney Seals, DJ10 Sports. Um, coach, first off, is there a favorite insect or a really interesting insect in one of those play calls or anything that we should know about? >> Uh, I don't think so. I think it's pretty uh pretty standard if you, you know, look on National Geographic or anything like that, you probably find it. So, yeah. >> And then also, Shotti told us a little while ago that he's been doing dinners for the players off the field. How are you trying to get to know them better? Yeah, I think you know it really the the easiest way is they come to the office a lot. You know they come a lot when they're you know have that downtime just to stop by kind of spend 15 20 minutes. Um you know we've done different events outside of here too. You're just trying to get to know the man before you you coach the player. Um and that's a constant process. Um might be phone calls, FaceTimes. You know me and Caleb were at the we weren't sitting together. We were at the game seven with the Thunder and the Spurs. So we're texting you know from other sides of the arena. You know it's different things like that. You know, it's a constant process. Um, it's not going to be a grand event that just kind of checks that box. You want to constantly make deposits when it comes to um relationships with your players. >> Brad Christian Bradsham, Cowboys Radio Network 1053, the fan pundits and trying to anticipate how the defense and you are going to perform say, "Well, he's never called a defense." How big a deal is that? And how much of a percentage of your job do you think that really is starting from now? Um, well, I mean, every play caller had to call his first game at some point in time, so I don't really think about that too much. Um, you know, it's going to be what it's going to be. You know, the expectations are, you know, whether I'm 65 and a 20 year play caller or or 34 in the first time when the result needs to look the same and so we take that serious. Um, so I don't really overthink that part of it. >> How much part of your job do you think play calling is? >> Huge part. Huge part. I mean, you know, we've talked about it, you know, things can sound great, you know, in the meeting room, um, on the practice field, that's a controlled environment. You know, when when it gets hectic out there, you know, I have to be the one to keep a calm mind. And also, whatever we've done up to that point to give the players the confidence to perform in whatever play call that we that we get to, um, we have to get to that point. So, um, you don't win without timely play calling, but more importantly, the fundamentals, the schematic knowledge, the techniques, those are going to make any play call come to life. So, you know, they're going to make me write more than I'm going to make them right. Um, and I'm very comfortable with that fact. >> Quick one from Todd. There's a lot of preconceived notions when it comes to this team and organization. Did you have any coming in here? And what have you learned about being with this organization the last four or five months? Um, well, I mean, I've been a a rival the last two years, so, you know, you kind of make stuff up in your own head to get yourself ready for a game. Um, whether it's true or not. So, um, no, I mean, it's it's first class. It's what you think. Um, what Jerry has built here is special. Um, his vision for what this franchise needs to be. Um, he has alignment. It's a crystal clear vision for all parties involved. Um, and that's something that I appreciate more than anything else. >> All right. Thank you. >> Thank you. So,

title: Klayton Adams: Evolution of the Offense  | Coaches Interview
text: How you doing? >> Good. How are you? >> How are you? >> Pretty good. >> Good to see you. >> Pretty good. It's great to see everybody. It's really good to see everybody. You know that. >> Ready? >> Do it. >> Calvin Watkins, Dallas Morning News. Uh, as you look at the offseason stuff and everything, how do you think your offense can evolve? Because obviously defenses are going to make the adjustments to what you did last year. Yeah, I mean we did a lot of studies in the off season just looking at things that maybe we were missing um or things that don't fit our personnel or things that we did that we didn't do enough. Um I think that's where you start. Um, I'm also kind of a firm believer that the the story of the season tends to ride itself. And, uh, it's one of the reasons I try not to to tie the screws too tightly to what you want to do in the offseason is because we're going to somebody's going to invent something accidentally in the preseason or in week six or week seven or week eight and then you're going to go, I want to do that. Um, that fits our personnel. Uh, or you're going to think of something that's off of something else you've done. So the league is always evolving and it evolves way harder and way faster during the season. So I I I do think a lot of that's it's going to happen organically. >> How much do you try not to overanalyze things because you say this is what we do best and that's what we're going to keep doing in comparison to maybe we need to tweak that a little bit. >> Yeah, I I try not to overanalyze. Um I my wife would tell you I under analyze uh probably closer to that. Um, but I I do think that just your reaction to things, you know, my my reaction to things tends to be pretty specific to like how how much I think you can grow in one area. And so, um, you know, exactly kind of like I said before is there's going to be something that, you know, I I went into my first season in Arizona like we're going to be an outside zone team. And then we ended up doing all sorts of other stuff. And last year I was pretty much, you know, I don't know how I feel about outside zone and then we ended up being decent at it. So, um there's uh topics like that all the way across the spectrum that we have an idea what we think we want to do and then somebody's going to play better than we think or you know you're going to have an injury or whatever it is and you're going to end up having to pivot. >> Clayton Todd Archer with ESPN. Dax talked about the red zone as a area of focus for you guys here because of issues last year. as you look back at it, what what were some of the problems in your mind? It wasn't like you got bad down there, but how do you get better in the red zone? >> Um, you know, I I think that cuz we really did kind of uh take it all in and say, "All right, let's be real honest with ourselves. Um, what do we need to do better down here?" You know, some of it was um I don't know if it's just maybe being young or performance anxiety, but like we we had more uh self-inflicted wounds in the red zone than we did in some other areas. You know, you if you have a negative yardage run on the one yard line like that, that's a lot different than a negative yardage run on the 50. Uh if you have a false start on the inside the 5 yard line, it's a lot different than a false start when you're on the minus 25. So, there was a little bit of that. Um there was, you know, a little bit of us just saying, "All right, like we were mainly run and action on normal down in distance out in the open field." And then sometimes we would get down there and kind of shift our thought process to more drop back stuff. Um, you know, I think specifically, uh, run gamewise, um, I think you got to find ways to use the 53 and a third in the pass game really and the run game. When you're when you're restricted to five or six yards, uh, vertically, you got to use your lateral space better. That's one thing that I'm always trying to um to to remind myself of. Um, and then I think, you know, just executing a little bit better. you know, there's there's never going to be like just the solution. Everything's going to be, you know, a small piece to the solution. >> Then, uh, being part of the accelerator program, what was that like to to go through that process and to think that, you know, however many years you've been in the league that you're now being viewed as a potential head coach? >> Uh, it was fun. It was unique. Uh definitely felt like I learned some things and and came away from it um I guess uh viewing some of the things that I know that I need to do better. I I guess with a little bit more urgency and not so much uh because you know whatever the the next step is it's because I I just want to be really good at my job here and and so sometimes those things can shed light on the things that you need to do better and it did that for me. John Modto with the athletic uh with Tyler Gayton. Just kind of what are you seeing from him in year three and just your overall assessment of your left hand spot? >> Um you know it's obviously it's always difficult to to evaluate offensive lineman when you're not wearing pads. Having said that, you know, just in regards to the things that he's supposed to be doing in the offseason, what he looks like, what his attitude is, how he answers questions. I think he's had an outstanding off season and I'm very excited, you know, to for for him to compete and for uh for us and him to have the opportunity for him to stay out there and and play and learn because that's you get better at football by playing football. And so uh regardless of whether it's the left tackle, the right guard, the starting safety, your you know your gunners on punt, like they got to be out there to get better and he's another person that falls into that category. And then at that running back position across the league, do you see it moving more towards how it used to be with like a Bellcow back or do you think it'll kind of blend a little bit? Maybe Bellcow, maybe a split back field. >> I think that that's just like very specific to to group by group. Um there are some guys around this league that are they are just totally good taking however 300 something carries or whatever per year. And then there are guys that are going to be a lot better if you know exactly where their limits are. I I just think it's specific. I think if you have that guy that you know like the Derrick Henry is is an example I always think of that like that guy's just out there every week and he takes a ton of carries and he's just bigger and stronger than everybody then I think that's the way you go. Um, I've always been a little bit more uh in places where, you know, you try to keep your your starting guy as fresh as you possibly can and spell them with another player. >> Nick Harris, fourstar telegram, you had said at the end of the season last year that you were really looking forward to diving in schematically, how you can maximize having the two wide receivers and what y'all can do with that as the evolution of that has played out this offseason. Is there anything you've learned? Anything you're excited to put on the field? Yeah, I think um it it really is kind of the way that the league is right now is that people are generally going to try to disguise from a two safety shell. Um you know, ours for whatever reason, not for whatever reason, I think we know what the reason is, but like ours isn't usually disguised. It's usually we get a lot of shell looks. And so just me coming from the places that I come from of sometimes you're overthinking like what if we get weak rotation here? What if we get this? You have to have those answers. Um, but I I guess they don't have to be nearly as specific if you're looking at a normal down and distance type play of all right, we can count on teams to play us a certain way and, you know, specifically because of who those guys are out there and who our who the guy that takes snaps for us is. Um, and so, yeah, I've leaned into that a little bit. Um, I think you also have to have answers, uh, because, you know, all sorts of things happen during the season and sometimes you're not playing with the same lineup every week. >> Um, Shotti has obviously had a lot of housework to do on the defensive side of the ball this off seasonason. He had said there were times where, you know, you would just pop into his office once a day and then that would be it. How was that process in the early parts of the offseason? You know, with the evolution of the offense, checking in with Shotti and how did that communication go? Yeah, it was I think it was good for for our offensive staff to kind of spend uh an off season, you know, just that way together. And and a lot of what we did last off season for good reason and and also, you know, it was great for me was just a blueprint of, hey, this is this is how I do it. Um and so that was really uh you know, like I've said before, it was really good for me to kind of step into that mold. And then this off season was a little bit more of a you know a good better how process on okay this is this is where we start and this is the root of it but you know what do I want to do what is my process look like how would I tweak it and I thought we got a lot out of some of the different things that we did. >> Joe White Dallas Morning News there was the most tight end draft in the last 20 years this year seems like the league really wants to go to 13 personnel or push for that for you guys obviously with the receiving core and how you kind of thrive in 11 personnel. How do you balance maybe the benefits of like seeking 13 personnel but also trying to play your best guys out on the field? >> Yeah, and you know, I think everything's got a time and a and a place. Um, obviously when you have two elite receivers, taking one of those guys off the field is usually, you know, you might get a greeting card from the defense uh afterwards. But I do think that there are uh there's a time and a place. And so, you know, as you get you get down inside the 10 yardd line and you're restricted for vertical space, having one guy out there can be a massive issue, uh, if you're trying to create extra gaps in your action game or your run game. So, you know, like I don't know that I see us being a team that's going to go out and do it 40% of the game, you know, like we did sometimes in Arizona, but I definitely see that as being a thing, a tool that we can use because, you know, those guys in that room do a nice job, too. And then Dak and C kind of talked about going up against Christian Barber's defense already and just kind of the disguise looks. What's been like just kind of the chess match already between your guys offense and going up against a new defensive coordinator? >> Uh it it's good uh just because you're going to see some different things at practice that generally you're not going to see until you get into the season. Um you know, I think that they've done a really nice job of kind of building it the right way. And um I've always said with kind of that family of defense, it it travels well around the league because it's fundamental and uh they they set edges. They they understand their checks in coverage. They play splits. Uh they coach things uh in coverage with very much detail and and they understand how to how to teach guys fundamentals and and apply those to techniques. >> Tommy, Tommy, Dallas.com. Last year you guys had Brock Hoffman as a guy who could go from guard to center and kind of fill in anywhere on the interior. Who are some of the guys that you view this year as guys who could play in multiple spots? >> Well, I think um you know TJ Bass is a guy that that we feel pretty comfortable um playing at at all those spots they're inside and he's proven that he can go in and give us productive time. Uh the other guys that are kind of in there competing and doing a good job and Trevor Keegan's been in there. Uh Nick's been in there uh working hard at it. Um you know, obviously our starting three uh and TJ, I think I think that's kind of the gist of the the guys that have been working in the interior. But you know, that's the you know, uh whenever a guy leaves us an opportunity for somebody else, you know, I think when I wasn't here, but I'm sure when when Brock and TJ were going in there for the first time, there's probably a lot of people who are nervous about it. So when those guys get their opportunities, they got to go out and and make it happen. >> I don't think we've spoken to you since the draft. What are your thoughts on Drew Shelton and what he can do? >> Yeah, I think I mean we'll find out a heck of a lot more when we get in pads. Um but just in in terms of the dayto-day and the way that he carries himself around the building, uh he has he has been what we've expected him to be so far. You know, when you're looking at a guy that's running around with no pads on, uh he's been accountable. Uh he looks athletic and has balance and body control and he's been smart and hardworking. So we need to go out in in pads and do the most important thing and then you can get a real evaluation on them. >> We'll finish up with two more. We'll go one from Garrett and one from Todd. >> Hey Clayton Garrett, CBS Sports. I know in the middle of last year when CD went down, you you and Brian said you discovered George Pickins can do more than just be an outside receiver. Kind of move him a little bit more around the formation. kind of what more can you do with that in your second season working with them and what do you think of his ability to operate inside and other spots beyond just outside? >> Yeah, I think uh you know year two is is a good opportunity to kind of force the issue on some of those things. Um so I think we'll we'll probably see more of that as we get into training camp of what he's comfortable doing, what he's not comfortable doing. But I do think that really the latter part of last year um not so much just like the the physical ability because I think that the physical ability like the the the guy can pretty much do anything. Um just you know putting guys in position where they're very comfortable operating. um you know is is really the big thing with him is uh and and when you take him off the backside of a 3x1 formation sometimes you you might be overthinking yourself a little bit with some of that stuff. And so um you know situation by situation probably not something that we would want to do every single play but he's certainly given us uh confidence in doing it with him. Brian was talking to us about having you do some pass game installs uh this year where last year you didn't do that stuff. He he kind of jokes like, you know, last year if I asked him to do it, he would been uh I don't know what's you know, he'd know it all. How much more I don't know aware or up up to everything what this past game is but in the last say 12 months. >> Yeah. I mean, it's it like as much as anything, uh, I coached tight ends in the NFL for two years, and so you you got to you got to have a pretty good idea what's going on to coach that position. You learn a lot of football coaching that position. For me, it was is was after going in the line room for two years, it was just kind of like a reawakening of, oh yeah, I remember uh what all this stuff is. And then and then really, you know, I I was walking into a terminology system that had been in place for a long time. And so, uh, it was really as much as anything kind of memorization of this is what we call this. Um, but it has been really good for me this off seasonason because I, you know, I don't know that I've ever been in a situation where even when I was the O line coach or I was the tight end coach or what the assistant O line coach, generally the installs are kind of broken up throughout the staff. And so, um, the the typical setup what you would get is, you know, whoever the coordinator is maybe installing the pass game and then whoever the offensive line coach is installing the run game and then guys installing kind of their their areas. Um, what was really good for me this off seasonason is with a lot of particularly the normal down and distance stuff is I wanted to install the entire thing and that was a good growing process for me and that's something that we'll continue to to do moving forward just because I think it helps me and I think it helps us. Right. >> Thanks everyone. Thank you. Thank you. Take care.

title: Joe Burrow Press Conference - June 17
text: Heat. Hey, Heat. Hey, hey, hey. You put it a lot of work these last couple days um after practice today. What's uh what's kind of been been about that? >> Just trying to get better, man. Just trying to get better. Um you know, nobody wants to get hurt in spring, so we're not doing a bunch of competitive reps. We're not, you know, we get 10 reps of seven on seven and then a bunch of individuals. So, um I'm just out there trying to get better. >> Would you like to get maybe a little bit more? How do you how would you like to balance that? Maybe >> I always push push for more. Uh, but now's now is certainly not the time for for injuries and if you do more competitive reps that opens that up. So, we'll get plenty of those in July, August. Uh, you know, we get better other ways. >> Joe, since we last talked to you, you've restructured your contract. Can you walk us through what that process was like and how does it feel to you for that to be done? Yeah, I think um you know it opened up some cap space which is good for us and you know I've been open about how I'm willing to do whatever you know they they need me to do to so that they can operate freely and we'll continue doing that as needed. >> Katie said that y'all had conversations kind of about how how you felt about things. How how maybe were those this year compared to maybe previous offseason, those conversations with the front office about what you wanted to see? >> Yeah, it's always open and honest. We got a great line of communication and uh you know, I think we're in a great spot. We filled just about every hole that we we've had. Um you know, operationally, we're improving. Um we're bringing in the right kind of people. I think, you know, for the most part, getting to know the rookies, they fit into to our culture and what we're trying to do here. So, uh, you know, we had a great off season. >> How are you trying to get better? >> Every way imaginable, mind, body, soul, just uh trying to improve myself and be there for for my teammates and build team camaraderie. and uh obviously I'm going to improve my my individual skills and strength and and speed, but um trying to build that culture and that that uh that vibe in the locker room that you need to win a championship is uh just as important. >> Do you work more on focus as you get older? Like focus on what you need to worry about and what you don't need to worry about. >> Yeah, I think specific I think it's uh It it's a challenge sometimes because when you're younger, you're just trying to improve every area of your game. You know, nothing is good enough. And to to some extent, that is still true, but um when you've hit a certain level, then you're trying to improve by this much instead of that much. And to do that, you have to get really nitty-gritty into the technical details of how your body moves, how you hold the ball, how the ball's coming out, uh your body position, when you're moving, and that can uh there's certainly cons to thinking about it that critically, and um now is the time to do it, not August. Uh so that's that's the rabbit hole I've gone down over the last, you know, four or five months. and um c certainly found some improvements but also you know found the the negatives that come with it. >> When did you decide and what led you to the uh to the decision of trying to build that camaraderie or being part of that or having a a bigger emphasis on that for you individually? >> Just just reflecting on where where I can get better and things that I can improve on to to help the team. >> How important can that work be Joe after practice? Not that it's the first time ever, but staying longer with the guys, the receivers, like how important is that for you and for them and and all that work? >> Um, you know, after practice is is mainly for me. Um, you know, guys typically like to to hang around and catch, but nobody's running routes a after practice. Mainly just spot catching. you know, guys will run a couple routes here and there that maybe uh the rep in practice wasn't exactly what we wanted against that look of of the defense and so we'll talk about it and then you know run one or two. But uh for the most part that's for me um thinking about my motion, thinking about um you know how I can improve throwing the football. >> I think you've been doing that after every practice at least that that I've attended and a lot of them have been deep balls. Are you like varying the arc and how you're throwing them? It seemed like you're experimenting a little bit. >> Yeah, that's that's you know, warm-ups after practice. That's what I'm doing. I'm experimenting with a lot of different things. You know, sometimes might not look pretty cuz I'm trying trying a lot of new things and um seeing how it works. Trial and error, that's the only way that you can get better. And so after practice, that's my time. >> How how is how you view team chemistry maybe changed or shifted as you went from last year to this year. Um you going back to the earlier question, how do you feel like you team chemistry now maybe differently than you did maybe before? >> I just think early in my career it was a lot easier. You know, we had a really young team. A lot of us had come in together and and been through it together. uh now we have so many varying ages on the team uh from guys that we're counting on and we've brought in some veterans too that certainly has made it easier but you know building trust between a 21-year-old first year player and a 31 32 year old 9 10 year vet that's that's a difficult task and job of the quarterback to try to to bridge those gaps where you can and that's something I've I've focused on. I think if you want to be a championship caliber team, then you have to build those relationships and build that trust. So, uh you know, you can have hard conversations about things that are going on on the field as well as off. >> Yesterday you were wearing a compression sleeve on your leg. Are you dealing with any injuries and how do you feel right now as far as like physical health? >> Yeah, I feel great. I feel great. Obviously, some days are better than others. Uh, you know, I've I've been through a lot, so some some days are going to be a little stiff and sore, so you try to find ways that make it feel better. >> When you were younger, first couple years in the league, how do you think that you earned that the trust that you were talking about? How do you think you earned that trust from the older guys around? >> Just with my work and then eventually with my play, that's really how you do it at the end of the day. you can do everything that you want off the field and impress, but if you don't do it on the field, that really doesn't matter. Um, but now is the time to try to prove yourself through your hard work and your effort and your attention to detail in meetings. And so that's the process the young guys are going through right now. And then obviously the next step will be training camp. How do you translate what you're doing off the field on the field? And then obviously the guys that have earned the right to play on Sundays will will do that and then they'll have to prove themselves again. >> How do you feel like the spring went for for you and the offense on the field and maybe anything that caught your eye? >> Yeah, I thought it was great. Um, you know, we have all the spots filled. Obviously, we have everybody all the starters back. So, that's a great a great feeling. We don't have uh any young guys, any new guys coming in that we really need to to count on. And so, the guys that are young that come in and and produce and perform. That's just kind of icing on the cake for us at this point. You know, it'll certainly be hard for for those guys to find a role this year considering how deep we are, but I'm excited to see who who will and who will help us. I think we there certainly are some guys that will be able to, you know, a couple receivers, couple tight ends, and then uh you know, we're deep at O line this year, which is exciting. Um and all the guys are putting in a lot of work to to try to improve. And then with the veteran players that we have coming back, they're doing a great job setting an example for for the younger guys and trying to teach them how to be great. So, I think the spring has gotten everybody better. and we need to continue that over the next month before we come back. >> Just going back to the Andre, >> man, Andre looks great this year. Andre looks unbelievable. He looks big, strong, fast. Uh he made a couple really nice contested catches in the spring this year in our limited reps. That's a big area of emphasis for him, I know. So, that was exciting to see and he's going to continue to to improve there. But um he looks uh just like he's playing with so much confidence. Confidence in his role, confidence in the offense and and and his ability. >> For you as a leader on this team, what did it mean? And how important is it that the attendance you guys had throughout this spring with the voluntary workouts and the OTAAS to have everyone in the building pretty much by by the time OTAAS got started and and to get this thing rolling early with the goals that you have for this season? Yeah, I just think, you know, it's important to to show up in these moments. There's there's a lot of improvement to be had from from these reps that we're getting and um phase two and phase three specifically. You know, we're on the field getting better for, you know, an hour, hour and a half. Those are valuable reps. Reps that you're not going to get if you if you weren't here. So, um, guys, guys realize that, guys, and that's why everybody >> are going down that rabbit hole. Joe, we talked about earlier. How much of that is thinking about not taking as many hits and protecting your body? >> Um, you know, certainly pops pops in here and there, but that's not uh that's not really my mindset currently uh this time of year. That'll be, you know, playing the game, how to play the game. That kind of comes in training camp. It's hard to to simulate that in your head this this time of year. There's no no rush. You know, your clock is always a little different in June than it is in September. >> When the pads come on, are there things you're looking forward to learning about the team and maybe what are they? >> Yeah, we'll we'll we'll see who's going to step up and especially on defense, we'll see. Excited to see how that new look defensive line feels in the pocket. Um, it's been fun to watch the communication of the defense in these walkthroughs that we've had. You know, who who's going to be vocal, who's going to step up into that leadership role. That's, you know, a lot of question marks, but we're going to set out to answer them. >> This gap between mini camp and training camp, how do you approach the next five or so weeks? >> Yeah, take take a little little break. Uh, and then, you know, once July hits, ramp it back up into the ramp up before training camp. Uh, you know, the next two weeks still be working out, but certainly not anything crazy. And then ramp it up in July. >> Joe, you guys have talked ago. You were asked, you were asked that and you were like, "It's go time. I have a reason." Why dial it back now and take that time? What? >> You live You live and you learn. Joe, you guys have talked a lot about being more explosive this year and the trend in the NFL. So many of these explosive teams are majoring under center. >> Can a team be truly explosive in the current NFL and not major in under center or is that something you have to have as a major part of your game? I think, you know, if you're going to be a gun team, you're going to get certain defenses and teams inherently are going to be more worried about the pass against us and try to take that away cuz that's that's what we're great at and teams know what we like to do and that we're really good at it. So, you know, trying to find ways to to be explosive in the run game and then try to find some things off of that that can get us a couple easy explosives and um you know, we're committed to that. Our coaching staff has done a great job this this off season of, you know, putting a plan together to try to execute that. So, I'm excited to see how it works out, but I'm always ready to to drop back 65 times and make it work, too. But but I mean isn't it is are what is it about that? Obviously it's your specialty and you guys have Jamar and T like obviously but like what is it about that that why you guys feel like it's just always been where you guys have leaned to just doing that rather than sprinkling in more of the under? >> It's what's been effective. It's been, you know, we we were heavy under center in 2020, 2021. That worked out well for us, but then we were so explosive that uh we stopped we stopped getting the defenses that the under center runs and the under center play actions were built for. Um and then we weren't explosive in the run game when we faced those light box defenses. So, you know, then we transitioned to a gun team and uh you know, our run game became our our RPOS's and our quick game basically and the run game was kind of icing on the cake because of that was effective for a couple years. Uh and then around 2024, you know, we got so good at just picking people apart underneath and marching the ball down the field that uh we started getting some more of the 2021 defenses. And so now we have to get back to making people pay for for playing that way against us. And that'll in turn then create that cycle again where we're explosive and then teams play a certain kind of defense and then uh we'll be more we'll be better equipped this this time to to be explosive in the run game to try to take advantage of that. >> Is it hard to look at trends around the league cuz you guys are so different than almost all teams like to say yeah well teams are doing it this way but yet they don't have what we have. Is that does that make it hard to kind of pick from what other teams are having success with? Well, it's certainly, you know, when you watch tape throughout the season, it's yeah, defense played this team this way, but you know, typically there's a trend of how teams play us compared to other teams and you know, always go into a game take I always take the film study that week with a grain of salt because um you know, we can get so many different things in so many different situations because of the guys that we have on the outside and how effective they are. Um, you always have to be ready for certain things that teams has have never shown before. >> Given all the moves that y'all made this off season, kind of how you kind of pushed a lot of gibs in that maybe normally y'all don't. Do you feel like if it's going to happen for you here, it's got to be this year given kind of where the contracts are at everything. Is it like this has to be the make or break? >> This is a lot of urgency, a lot of urgency this year certainly. Um, you know, we have everything we need. We were deep at just about every single position on on the team. You know, we've talked in the locker room this year about, you know, years past, you know, you wonder who's going to make the team. Uh, and it was topheavy and you wonder about the bottom the bottom guys and this year it's guys that were once that top level that were, you know, they're on the team for sure. Now there's a lot of competition at those spots on the, you know, 53, 54, 55, uh, at the at the end of that list. So, um, this is the first year that is really the case in my opinion and it's an exciting place to be when you have too many good players. Uh, so we're going to have to now it's our job to try to find a way to make this a cohesive unit and like I said before, build that trust and build those relationships so we can go out and execute. >> So, when you have that level of urgency, you got that level of talent, what do you feel like you guys have to accomplish to make sure that you capitalize on both of those feelings? We're we're going in expecting to win every game that we step foot on the field. Uh there's certainly uh obviously, you know, you want to win a Super Bowl, and that's certainly the plan. Um but you got to take it one day at a time, one week at a time, and you know, I'm excited for the journey. >> You say we've got everything we've need. We've got everything we need. You talk about the things that are in place right now, the competition that exists. Is there any added level of pressure that comes with understanding what you have here in the building? >> I hope so. I hope so. I think that's great. You know, put put pressure on guys. I love it. I thrive in it. We'll find out who else does. Um I know that we have the kind of people that want to be in that spot. You know, I want I want everybody talking about the Bengals. I want everybody talking about what I'm saying in my press conferences. Is he, you know, you go back and watch what I said before 2019 season at LSU. You know, I feel very similarly about this team. Uh, you know, I'm so excited to get started and and get get moving and I wish we would ramp this ride into training camp so we can continue to improve. uh because I feel like, you know, there's so much greatness that we're going to be able to achieve this year. I'm just excited to get going. >> You said the way that you talked then is similar to the way that you talk now. Is the way that you felt then similar to the way that you that you feel now? >> I certainly feel that way about this team. I think, you know, we've we have guys that have been there and done that and also guys that have had a lot of individual success and not necessarily the team success that are looking for it. um guys like Dexter and guys like Jonathan and you know bringing the guys like that in is that's so advantageous to a lot of different people young players trying to improve makes it easier for coaches. Um you know we have so many guys with so much talent, you know, I'm just excited to put it all together. >> Back to the culture thing. Do you do you think uh you've become a little bit looser in the locker room? Just maybe joking around a little bit, maybe showing your humor, or do you think you've >> No, I think the opposite. I think I've I think this off season I've really focused on, you know, trying to to bring urgency to the room and try to uh just get everybody to understand the the level of urgency that we have this year, the level of play that is going to be required of every individual that steps foot on that field. So, I've tried to communicate that. I've tried to be a little more vocal, maybe in a mean way. Uh, I think that's a little out of my comfort zone, but that's that's somewhere that I'm improving. And um maybe maybe it's good, maybe it's bad. I don't know. We'll find out. But >> you said it mean >> Yeah. Um, but yeah, like I said, I'm just trying to bring urgency to to every room that I step in and uh try to foster an environment of improvement. >> You you wanted a high level at every level of football you ever played at high school national championship at LSU. You know, the Bengals took to the Super Bowl didn't close the deal close. Is winning the Super Bowl all that you care about right now? I mean, is that the the primary goal. >> Yes. >> And what's it going to take to get that done? >> You know, all the things that that we've talked about, you know, fostering that relationship in the locker room, fostering trust between coaches and and players, trying step in, trying to uh improve myself and show everybody what it takes to improve and be great, you know, all these things. >> Competition. Did you watch the Knicks in there and >> I did. >> You thinking about Did that make you think about the venture you guys are on? >> Yeah. Well, anytime you get a chance to watch somebody win a championship, that's uh an exciting thing. That's where we all want to be. That's what we all want to experience and many of us have. And once you have, then you'll do anything to get back there. to have the kind of competition that you were talking about a little bit earlier at the bottom of the roster with how good it is. How important are those guys, you know, 50, 51, 52, 53 to, >> you know, winning a championship and winning those games where you don't know how it might go down the stretch and something might pop up? How how much of a key is that for you guys to have good guys all the way through 1 through 53? >> That's so important. You know, you see every year, you know, there's a big play on special teams that that sways the game a certain way. You know, you saw several games in the playoffs where, you know, somebody knocks a ball out on special teams, somebody um muffs a punt on special teams. You know, you have to have guys that you can count on because they're going to be in those spots. And if you have guys that can make plays in those spots, it's a game changer. >> Two non football questions for you. Do you plan to watch Joe Flacco on quarterback since you were just recently on it? And >> I don't think so. And will we see you at any of the World Cup games when you saw Mahomes at the game last night? And are you a soccer fan? >> Yeah, I I watched the World Cup. It's certainly exciting. You know, I'll probably be Yeah, I was uh >> Yeah, you'll see me somewhere. >> Watch me hatrick last night. >> I I was I watched the first goal and then I fell asleep. Got a little too late for me. What does uh mean leadership look like? >> Uh just if something isn't up to a standard, then calling it out right then and there, maybe a little louder than I than I have in the past. And that's uh growth as a leader that you maybe I keep doing it, maybe I don't. I don't know. But certainly try it out and just try to bring a little intensity to the room. >> What are the what are your teammates reactions to that change in leadership style? >> Yeah, it's been great. I think just uh the urgency overall has uh improved in general. Um you know that maybe that played a part, maybe maybe it hasn't, but uh something I'll keep trying. Is there anyone that you kind of like consult with to, you know, think about how you should go about, you know, being a leader in strategies that you do that or was that just kind of, you know, you sit at home in your thoughts and you're like, I I I want to do this. talk to you guys on the team and see what you know what's needed out of me, what's needed um in certain spots, what where um >> yeah, guys on the team do a good job of uh vocalizing what what we think the team needs. >> You notice that the players on the team have responded to your leadership? I mean, you have done an unbelievable job uh being here and they seem to, you know, really uh really respond to what you're trying to get done. Are you sensed that? >> Yeah, I think so. Uh, you know, guys have responded really well to to certain things and um we have a lot of guys that that want to be better. >> See, Dexter said you guys watch some basketball, I guess. >> Yeah, me and Dex have been kicking it a lot. >> Is that something that's out of character, too? Did you spend some time with some guys on the other side? >> Um, probably more so than I have in the past. Uh, you know, like I said, it's helped, you know, that we've brought some some veteran guys in here that, you know, can help me do that. You know, Dex has been amazing. Getting guys getting guys together, trying to build that that off the- field relationship that you need. >> What do you guys do? >> Whatever. Nothing. Nothing specifically. Usually watch whatever game is on. >> Did you ever play soccer growing up? It was my first sport I ever played, but switched quickly to baseball. >> Position. >> I don't think there were positions back then. >> How old were we talking? >> Uh, I mean that was like first, second grade. >> Thank you, sir. >> Thank you, sir. Have a good summer. Would you make a game again? Heat. Heat.

title: Zac Taylor Press Conference - June 17
text: [music] >> Back? >> Everybody. >> Charles, first off, any injuries to note coming out of mini camp? Anybody that getting nicked up? >> No, nothing new. >> Okay. >> Guys still progressing through the program and we'll see where they're at once training camp comes along, but we got out with no new injuries, so that's good. >> What led to the decision to cut things short by a day or so? >> That was a decision I made last week, really. We we got in everything we wanted to get done. We got all the installs in. I thought the guys did a great job getting the work in on the field over the, you know, since really late late April when we started meeting and lifting. And then all the field work we've done in May and June, we accomplished everything we set out to accomplish. Um I thought the coaches have utilized every minute we're on the field. I thought they did a great job with the practice plans and the reps. So, I just felt like we were in a good space and ended on a high note. Let these guys come back in late July. >> So, I think you all went longer, used the full time, the allocation of three days. What did you, I know you just mentioned a little bit, was there anything extra that you saw this year that said, "Okay, we really felt like this this is why the work was so good?" >> Well, we probably utilized more phase two time than we have in the past. So, we we've been on the field for for a good amount of time and got a lot of good work in. We're not really physical with the 11-on-11 stuff. And so, at at some point you just reach a point of diminishing returns where you're out there and we've accomplished a lot of work and now it's time to take a break and then come back in training camp ready to roll. >> It's kind of a trend. We've seen that, I know San Francisco, LA canceled it completely. Is there a reason behind you think why we're seeing that more across the league, something like that? >> I would guess uh those two specific teams are maybe reporting earlier because they get to report sooner because they play that Wednesday game. So, that might have factored into there as I can't I can't really speak to that, but I just know it was the right fit for us right now and I think our guys are really excited. >> What have you seen from the defense in off-season? >> I think you saw a lot of year-two development from a lot of guys, year-two in the system development. So, that's great to see from all those guys that are returning that we've got high expectations for. I thought that the leadership that the new guys have brought in, you know, the free agents that we signed has been tremendous. They've picked it up fast. They played a lot of ball. So, they understand it very well. So, I just thought they the chemistry, the communication um has really stepped up on that side of the ball and it's really good to see. >> Did you like the fact that there wasn't a lot of drama? Seemed like that everybody was about their business. I mean, that's just from the outside. It just seemed like a very standard, run-of-the-mill, and that can be a good thing obviously if you're >> It is. It's a great thing. A lot of the drama often times is is outside drama. You know, inside we're we're usually pretty clean with it. Guys go about their business, but um I feel like everybody is really focused, showed up, got the work in that we needed them to get, and and so now it's time to move on. >> Was there one moment or one thing, one reason that you came that you you realized okay, we're going to cut it. You said you decided last week. Was there one >> We've gotten through all of our installs now. There's not one moment, but we've just gotten through all of our installs. The guys have come in and they've worked hard. And so, again, you you can always steal more reps and do all that stuff, but I just thought it was time to throw the guys a bone and send them away for the summer. >> How did you let them know what was their reaction? >> I think that they I told some guys last night. I'm sure that that seeped through overnight. Um so, when I told them this morning officially, it was a little anticlimactic. But, for the most part, yesterday some guys knew. >> What Will you be watching Joe Flacco on quarterback? >> I've kind of already watched Joe Flacco on quarterback, so I feel like I've seen it. >> [laughter] >> Entertaining. You get to I think you really get to see um a lot more about him, you know, and it's I I it's fascinating cuz he's such a great guy, great teammate, so much fun to be around, really enjoys the whole process. I mean, he just enjoys playing football and he just enjoys being in the locker room. And he's kind of said all that kind of that stuff up here is um some of those quotes that he had that really took off last year, but I think that'll just really shine through. I think uh I don't want to ruin it for I don't want to ruin the show for anybody, so I'm not going to speak more to to what's on there, but it's entertaining. >> Did you learn more about him than you already knew from coaching him for a year? >> No, but you got to realize I I don't ever get to see in the huddle in a game. Um a lot of the bench conversations the players have from player to player, you don't get to see all that. So, there's you all see a lot more during a game than I do. Um I'm I'm almost the worst seat in the house at times, you know, you can't see the full field and so sometimes when you get to see stuff like this, it's entertaining cuz it fills in some of the some of the blanks from the games that we've had. >> What did you want to see from the offense this spring? >> I think Pitch has done a great job articulating what we expect from our guys. Um to be more explosive, to be able to close out games, you know, in our 4-minute drill, and that's going to take place on the ground primarily. And so, I think our guys have really bought into what it needs to look like for our team next year. It's not just speaking to the offense, it that that's a team aspect of it where we need all three phases to be intertwined in order to play in each phase how we want to play. Obviously, on defense, you want to get a lead and you can just tee off and we can finish games with a lot of the playmakers we have up front. And on offense, you want the defense to play really well so we get that lead and we get able to get to grind it out, control the clock, and finish the game on the run, and wear down a defense, and special teams be explosive and win the battle of field position. So, it all ties together. We're all counting on each other to be able to step up and do their job. And so I will just I think that's just going to continue to ramp up and I've been really pleased with Al and the rest of that staff. >> What have you seen from Al Colby Young? >> Continuing to grow. I'm really pleased with with the baseline that he started with when he came in here. Very eager, great personality, willing to do everything it takes. Um what works against Colby is the years of experience around him. Everybody's done it all and so there's not a lot of mistakes happening around. I'm not even saying he's making mistakes, but just everything's going to be nuanced on exactly how we want it done. He's eagerly doing it. Um really pleased with the direction he's headed. And really excited to see him put the pads on cuz I think that's going to be a huge advantage for him. His physicality and being able to separate with that physicality, his run after the catch. Um he's got really strong hands. So I think I think some of his best traits will show up when the pads come on. But um he's done everything we've asked and so I'm I'm just excited to see him get some opportunities and see what he can do when the pads come on. >> How big has it been to have Dexter here throughout the off season program and just get him acclimated with >> I I think just to to, you know, lead by example. You know, instead of saying things and not being around, he's he's been here front and center. I don't know if he's really left since the day he showed up in the trade. >> Yeah. >> Um so it's just really good to have veteran leadership like that. That's that's been in the building, been around. I has experienced a lot of things over the the seven years he's been in the league. Um that he can bring to the table along with a lot of these other vets that we've signed and acquired and brought in and so I I just think that the leadership on that side of the ball has really expanded amongst the amount of players that we have. I I think you'll see big jumps from some of the guys that have been here in the program for the last couple years. And so I'm really pleased with the direction that that that leadership is going on defense right now. >> Does it take long for free agents for you to notice that the leadership and the leadership >> Not this group. They're they're not bashful about it. They They know what they want and they know how to get there and they know what they need from their teammates. And so I think there's there is a humbleness from this group, but there's also a I'm not waiting around to feel my way through this before I start speaking. They've done a really good job of saying what needs to be said um because they're confident how they go about their business, the work they put in. and so it's it's just been really great for me as a head coach to be able to see those guys come in and and act that way. >> What do Dexter and now what what do Dexter and Jonathan Allen give you in the middle of that? You know, it's kind of jumping off that point about experience and leadership. >> Yep. I I think um kind of lost with the physical talent that they both bring is is the above the neck. The alignments they see in the backfield, the weight on the guard's hands, how the center's holding the ball. All that kind of stuff they've seen over the course of their career that is a learning process. You don't just walk in the league and know that. Some guys maybe coming from college have a little bit of a head up there, but um I think those guys just understand the nuances that us coaches spend a lot of time studying and understanding cuz we've been in the profession for so long. So those two along with BJ and TJ in the middle there's so much veteran knowledge there that they utilize to put themselves in the best position and they can communicate to those around them so those guys can play even faster because they know what's coming. >> They seem to have walked in with kind of like they had already had season on their chest, the way they kind of walked in. >> And football's football. I mean, they they've been in the scheme. They they've run all this stuff before. So it makes sense to them. That might be just different terminology, but they they know how to do it, when to do it and they know how to make those around them better. to where they might not always get the production, but they can make sure the linebackers get the production behind them cuz they play clean. They make sure the ends around them you know, they're picking their ends guys and the ends are coming underneath and getting a lot of production. So, those guys it's it's sometimes it's it's a a very selfless job you have in the interior because the production doesn't always come on the stat sheet. But, you can do a great job without the production because the guys around you are playing very clean and you're winning games and and holding teams to very few points. And I think a lot of I mean, I say that out loud. I'm thinking about Dexter last year. If you look at you know, I think it was what half a sack or one and a half sacks. That doesn't show up on the tape. It's it's just constant havoc in the pocket on tape and guys around him getting production um that he has created. And so, that's we need that from all those guys and and we'll be a great team. >> Going against guys like >> Cam Heyward, Chris Jones, Calais Campbell, guys that have interior played really well as they've gotten older. Has your opinion changed on how long to expect high levels of play >> A long time. I just look at the age of all these guys. It's like some of them play their best football later on. Now, you got to take care of them. You know, that's my job, you know, in training camp in the off season to take care of them so they can go out there on Sunday and be at their best. But, they figured out the body maintenance part of things at this point in their careers. Um and and they just have the knowledge that allows them to play their full potential. They're not just out there just put their head down and trying to create havoc. They they there's an intent behind everything that they do. And just hearing the communication when I stand over there in the walk-throughs and I hear Jonathan Allen say something. He's seeing something as soon as we line up, you know, and that's um you're always going to have tendencies that way, but really good defensive players they they cut the playbook in half on offense second you line up based on the backs alignment, tight ends alignment. They can look at the guards and get some indicators there and so, it'll be good for us as an offense too to hear some of that. Hear some things that that we can continue to tweak and um that's just a huge asset that that probably is undervalued, you know, often >> What kind of impact do you think Bryan Cook will have on Jordan Battle? >> I I think he's got a big impact. He's played at a high level for a number of years now. I think Jordan Battle has really grown as a player and as a leader as well. And so I think those two guys will really feed off each other. They got they both have really tremendous personalities. They're not shy. Neither one of them I'd say was shy. So I I think they're only going to make each other better. >> Zac, is he kind of on track to be ready for camp? >> I don't want to make any predictions on that, but he's done a great job and moved along as as we'd hoped he would.
