I think I mean the biggest thing is he haven't I mean we could talk about you know phase three mini camp. You know football is played with pads on and um like I said with the way I train the way I try to get my body ready I I'll show him that you know maybe I could go six plays instead of the four that they talking about. Um, but like I said, that's the that just the that's my mindset, you know, but I'm I'm not gonna I played four snaps and he s me out. I'm not gonna be over there, you know, why in the hell you taking me out or thing in that nature cuz that's a distraction. I think um like I said maybe two second year player Jeff maybe I would have been like pissed off like but I think when you like I said in this style of defense running out the stack I mean you like I mean every day like you see Solomon probably getting like 2700 yards a day that because he running out the stack and things of that nature. So that's the standard and so um I mean whenever that time come we'll see but like I said we got a long way for that >> the individual work the last two days is that you more catching up to speed getting back in shape and rhythm or is that more being careful of that elbow or something else? >> I mean we just worked out a plan. We had a great plan coming in, you know, just to stay out of the team reps and, you know, just work work on things on the side, of course. But like I say, it was me and me and coach Sol was was on the same page of that and we worked out a plan for me to be able to get still get my work in. Um, you know, I kind of regretted wearing a helmet out there on the side like that, but especially today. Um, but no, it was good just to be able to even be out here warming up with the guys and then getting my uh work in on the side. But um, yeah, it was a plan that we talked about. Um, of course, but wouldn't say so much of trying to nurture the elbow. U, like I said, this got the elbow. That's what back in February, like everything is feeling good, but like I said, come training camp, I'll be out there ready to roll with the guys. >> Jeff, what do you, what do you feel, what do you view as a successful season for yourself in 26? >> Um, I, you know, I haven't thought so much about the season. Um, you know, I feel like that's like that hurdle down the road. um you looking ahead, you may trip over that one. So, I really haven't thought so much about the season. You know, my biggest goal, especially coming off last year, I would say, you know, I want to win. The biggest goal is to win. Um I think that's the only thing I could speak on right now outside of like I said, I don't want to look too far ahead. I have what we got after tomorrow, I think it's 47 days. How can I be the best Jeffrey when I leave here after tomorrow, come back July 28, ready to roll. So, like I said, I'm not so focused on the season just yet. Maybe after training camp, you can ask me that question, I'll have a better idea. >> Wrapping up offseason program. Feel different this year compared to maybe last year when you were rookie. >> Um, I think you just have a better understanding of how the whole process of the season from, you know, this part of the offseason all the way to the end of the season works. Um, so you just have better perspective, um, and know what you need to do and when you need to do it. How do you feel like it's gone for you? >> Yeah, I think it's gone very well for me. I think I made a lot of improvements this year. Um, and I'm just building on what I showed on the field last year and trying to take steps forward from there. >> What are some of those things you've worked on specifically? >> Uh, I think a lot of the problems I had last year came from like my posture. Um, and like how that can lead to being more aggressive overall. Um, and so that's something that I've been working on a lot this offseason. >> How do you how do you fix your blocks? Uh, just try to have a crazy coach in the offseason that, you know, beatsit out of you, makes you tired, and then tries to make you have good posture when you're tired even. Um, so yeah, that's what I've been trying to do. >> Here or away from >> uh been away from here. I actually train with Wellell um and if you've noticed, he has very good posture very often. Um, so training with him and our trainer has been a big thing for me. If you're if you're the fourth or fifth guy in this in this group, what how do you envision your your role? What's that guy need to >> Uh I don't know. It's not really up to me to decide what my role is. Um I would never envision myself as that in general, but uh like I said, it's not up for me to decide that. >> How do you like the opportunity to have to work with Greg Lewis? He's a guy that's been there and done that, played your position. How much do you feel he can help you out? >> Yeah, he's done a great job. Um he honestly is a a great coach on and off of the field. Um so I've really appreciated having him here. >> You kind of reflected back on the rookie year. You kind of alluded to it. Did you feel like you hit a wall? Do you kind of feel like something slowed down with all the reps? Just kind of what is your review of rookie year for you? Um, yeah, like I said, I think, uh, there was times when I just wasn't being like fully myself in terms of like aggression and like attacking every rep. Um, and so, like I mentioned, that's something that I've been working on a lot this offseason. >> You mentioned Juan Dale. Um, just how beneficial has he been being in the system before for the rest of the receiver? >> Yeah, obviously he he knows the system like the back of his hand and we don't. Um, and so having them out there, like being out there and having him next to you like gives you a little bit of confidence knowing like, hey, if I don't know the like, he's going to let me know. >> How complicated is the system? >> I wouldn't say it's complicated, quote unquote, but there's a lot of stuff that you need to know. Um, and so it's just the learning curve is a is steep, but I think like once you know everything, you'll be fine. >> How good you are now? I think I have a very good grasp of what the offense is now. Um, but like I said, when Dale's out there, like you can you have that extra added level of confidence? >> How different is it from the system you ran last year or the system you ran in college? Are there any similarities? >> Um, I mean like con conceptually football is football, but I think like the operation, you know, like how you execute the plays is quite a bit different than what I did in college um and last year. Um, I think just like the speed of the execution is is the biggest difference. Um, like as you've noticed, we're always up on the ball. Like it's go go go go go until maybe you have like a net zero play and then you slow down a little bit from posture. Do anything different this offseason from weight? Try to work on speed, size, anything different for you head into year two? >> You said weight, speed or size? >> Yeah. >> Uh, no. I think those are all like at good levels for me. I mean, obviously you always want to try to get faster. Um, but I don't know if that's going to move the needle that much. >> You feel like you play faster. >> Yeah. I mean, that's a lot of that's to do with posture as well. >> You talked last year about how quick the ball was on you with Cam. You need to be ready for it in this offense. How much does does that serve uh what what Dave Wall's trying to do? >> Oh, I see. Yeah. So, I mean, I think Daveball is doing a really good job of playing to Cam's strengths, which that is one of them. Um, and so I think there's been like a good meshing of, you know, Dave's opinions and Cam's opinions and, you know, like coming to compromise there. So, I think, uh, he's been doing or they have been doing a really good job of working together. >> These routes you're running and stuff, the ball being on you fast is especially important. >> Sorry, what was that? >> The ball being on you fast especially important in what you're doing now. >> Is it important? Um, it can be depending on the play. >> Said a couple of days ago that the difference isn't that the field is slowing down, it's that the plays are faster in this offense. >> What does that mean? How are the plays faster? >> Yeah. Um, without giving away too much, uh, >> I just think, like I said, you know, Cam has a very specific play style, um, which is getting the ball out as fast as possible. And so, like I also said, Daves has done a good job of like listening to how Cam wants to run things. You know, like you might have one concept in this offense and one concept in another offense that are the exact same, but like the execution might be more tailored towards how Cam sees football as opposed to something else. >> How's it been getting to know Carnell and maybe any you've shared to help his transition? >> Has it been getting to know him? Yeah, he's been a great rookie. Um, he's been doing an awesome job. um to be honest like I no matter I try to eat meet or treat everybody like peers. Um and so as much as I can teach him he can teach me and so I think like overall a receiver room is super tight. >> Let me slide one more posture again. When you when you look back at your posture, whether it was last year at Stanford, I mean, were you how would you describe what it looked like then? Were you slouching at the line of scrimmage or >> No, I think it's more about being forward like having a forward lean to like honestly every like there's not there's really not a phase of the game where you shouldn't be at a forward lean. Um like maybe if you're running like a 40 yard route or you're down the field trying to track the ball. Um, but it's really about like having your nose forward, your body forward. Um, staying low in in and out of routes especially. Um, yeah. >> Thank you. >> Thanks. Thanks. >> How much farther along do you feel uh from draft night? >> Oh man, I feel uh extreme I feel extremely like extremely better than I than I came in. Um, I didn't got, you know, halfway acclimated. I haven't got it all the way yet, but uh I didn't I didn't got to the point where I feel comfortable um just going out there and playing with the guys. Um you know, the plays and stuff as far as the plays, I mean, those feel like um like I know them like the back of my hand uh right now. So, um now it's just taking that next step into just, you know, becoming, you know, the caliber player I think I am. It's uncommon >> for the coaches to have the refs blow sack plays dead at practice. How much did you guys like that today? >> That was that was that was smooth. In college, they ain't do that. We ain't do that in college. We was we was the offense the offense bombed us and we we thought we had a sack. Nah, it was a bomb. It was no sack. So, I I mess with that. >> What about from a technique standpoint and just how you maybe you've improved as a player? Have you learned some things over the last couple months? >> Uh, definitely. Um, as far as how we play stuff up here, it was totally different from when I was in college. So, like, um, I I really had to start from ground zero and, uh, just get the fundamentals of how we, you know, how we got off the ball. Um, especially in the in the attack front that we in. Um, I felt like it took me it took me a week, maybe two, to get to get that part down, but once I got that part down, everything else came a little easier. >> With that attack, like that mindset, like that's what's asking you to do. You don't have to read too much and see. How much does that excite you to be able to just pin your ears back and go get? >> Man, that's uh that's that's what I like that's what I wish I, you know, really could have did in college. No, I don't get me wrong. I love what I did in college, but if I could have just got off the rock like how like how I am now, uh, man, it it it would have been a really really fun year. Like, it would have been a really fun couple years. It was still fun, but I I like I really love playing in this type of defense. >> What do you think of some of the things that White Cotton and Tanzel Smart that they're doing with you? of, you know, the the uh the ball they throw it at you to make sure you get your hands up and the football on the string and all those things. >> Straight eye discipline. Um everything we do is off our discipline. Um if you if you watch our drills, you see us keying the ball. Um he he say we don't move until that ball move. So he throw any distractions. He can push us. Uh you see you see sometimes he even throw the tennis ball at us like but he just like that just you know he just building he's just callousing us in that uh in the in the like watching that ball keying that ball and whenever it flinches we gone. >> Was there was there a moment or a rep where it kind of clicked for you that this is the kind of defense you fit in or that this is the kind of defense that's more fun for you than what you were talking about? >> Uh it really wasn't even a rep. It was just me, you know, looking through the install of it. Um, you know, when you when you just watch the tape and you see guys just getting go go go go go and it's really not nothing else to it but go. I mean, I don't I feel like I don't feel like any D lineman would say no to that. Like, nah, we any D lineman would love to just go every play. >> What is your focus or plan these next 40 days leading train camp? uh one to figure out um what what I need to improve on as far as um how my offseason went up here and then from there is just um you know just adding adding more adding more to me. Um I want to make sure that I come in polished uh in shape uh and ready to go. Um, I'm going to stay in the playbook, uh, get training, and then I'm going to make sure that I work the fundamentals that, you know, we do every day up here every day. >> When you think about from the mental side, how have you been able to maybe grow and develop in that way outside of the physical? Um the mental side uh I say just being up first it's the first time that I've been away from home for like you know a further away from home. I went to Auburn and I was an hour away from my from my house. So I mean it really wasn't like it really wasn't too much of a difference for me. But whenever I came up here, it was the more free time, the the more the the the longer I was, the distance away I was from my family. And then, you know, it just it just was showing me that I had to really lock in on like this. Um, when I was in college, I mean, I could go home every weekend. I could, you know, if I wanted to, I could have went home every day after practice. I mean, I was just that close. But up here, it's like I'm focusing on me and I'm focusing on ball. So, um, really I feel like that was better for me just to focus on ball. >> We've seen you work with Tanzel before practice a couple times. That's not just him. It's some veterans obviously deep position. What's it like to, you know, go from a coach to then Jacob Martin maybe help pulling you aside and helping you out with some handwork and >> stuff to have those resources? >> Oh, no. That's that's great. Like, uh, just to have those resources is great. Um I take that I take that as just picking everybody's brains. Whenever you know Germaine came during uh OTAAS uh I was picking his brain all the time when you know Jacob Martin he was here. He was here every practice and I was picking his brain every day just to make just you know get the knowledge of like how he do stuff. We don't play the same at all. We don't play the same at all. But just to get a different perspect perspective on like how to play Dline or how to rush a passer is um is is is like key for me because I I'm still developing that that pass that passers package for me. >> With Jeff Simmons, you're in the building with him now. How has that been just being able to gather things from him and just learn how to be a pro from a guy that's done it so well? >> Uh man, it's been great. Like you said, he's a pro and like he's been seasoned in it. like he knows what it's like to to to play here and um I feel like he knows a little bit about like I mean he definitely knows a little a lot more than what I do especially uh playing in the league and um man it's it's like just coming on the sideline I mean uh I I don't really think he practiced um these last two days but just coming to the sideline and just like you know getting his perspective on like things he's seen that I could do better on you know as far as uh when the old lineman is jump setting I mean, I got a good get off. I got to be able to plant that foot in the ground and come back inside on it. Um, and it's just things I couldn't see myself on the field that he seen off the field. And I was like, you know, just picking that picking that up from him like it is great cuz I mean, so he, you know, really wanted the best to do it. So, it's like you got no choice but to like, you know, really lock in and listen to him. Cody, what's the dynamic for you, you know, being a veteran trying to get yourself ready to go, but at the same time working with some of these younger guys like Hill, like Hill and some of these other guys. >> Yeah. You know, I'm going to my eighth year and, you know, this is in the first arm around. So, you know, I know what I need to do to get myself ready, but also at the same time, the things I've experienced, things I've learned along the way, you know, I'm trying to help these young guys, you know, give them some wisdom, things I've learned along the way, and just help them, you know, catch up to speed and just being a pro in general. Coach Salah described you as your presence on the field this week in the offseason is kind of like riding a bike when it comes to being a veteran on this team but also learning new defense, new players, new teammates. How has this year been different in years past for you? >> Um difference wise, you know, it's been hard, but it's been good. You know what I mean? It's challenged all of us physically, mentally, but um I would just say, you know, coming in coming into this team with, you know, whether you're new, whether you've been here, um with the new staff, you know, there's high expectations, there's high standards, everyone wants to, you know, show out and look good for the new staff, you know, so um you know, this spring so far or I guess this conclusion of it now, but it's been highly competitive. It's been fun and you know, there's the offense looking great. I think defense's looking great as well. Special team's looking great and so um I'm excited for what's to come. Tell me like some of the guys around you, whether veterans up front or behind you or some of the draft picks that have come in. >> Everyone's a good group. Really good locker room. A lot of good guys, you know, whether young or old. I mean, you know, everyone's seeming to to mesh well. You know, it's a good locker room, like I said, and just uh um you know, I'm going to say it again. I'm excited for what's to come. >> With this defense, seeing you know, guys CJ Mo, see Dre Green Law, Brett Warner, etc. Like what they've been able to do, how much does that excite you to be able to to play in that same? >> Yeah, it excites me a lot. you know, looking back as soon as they hired him, you know, I I I was looking back at all the linebackers that have played underneath him. Of course, I knew, you know, about the San Fran guys, you know, I was playing against those guys my first four years of my career and so, um, you know, great track record as far as linebacker play in this defense and so, you know, that made me really excited and just getting able to do it in the spring, you know, getting getting the feel of it, getting the reps. Um, you know, it's it's fast, it's physical, and, you know, I'm looking forward to it. >> What is it that makes him so conducive to linebacker success? >> Just a lot of his vision and breaking. So, a lot of it's just top down and just being able to play fast and physical. You know, everything's, like I said, being top down. You know, a lot of your visions on the quarterback and so it's able to just, you know, run and hit and that's what a linebacker wants. >> What are your impressions? >> He's going to be a good player. You know, he's athletic. He can run. Um, I also like him too in the film room. You know, he's eager to learn and he's receptive of of coaching and of teaching. And so, um, you know, he's going to be a really good player in this in this league. when a guy is drafted at your position in the second round, like how do you look at that? And yeah, how how do you approach that? Like in terms of >> um That's a good question. You know, I approach it the same way I approach anything. You know, I'm still going to, you know, show up here as a professional, still work hard, still do what I need to do, but also at the same time, um I'm looking to help him be the best the best player he can be. You know, I was the roles were reversed when I was a rookie, when I was drafted Seattle. You know, it was it was different. you know, there's older guys in the room and um the way those guys took me in and taught me how to be a pro, taught me, you know, nuggets of the game, if you will. Um you know, I'm I'm just doing the same thing and passing that knowledge along. >> What did you like about what you did last year, what are ways you think you can be better this year? >> For me, last year, I had a phenomenal year in the pass game. You know, I thought I was one of the best coverage linebackers in the game, but um didn't like my run game last year. And you can argue scheme to scheme, whatever. It doesn't matter either way. I I didn't like it. And you know this year emphasis for me is is the run game. >> How can you get better at that during the offse? >> Just being aggressive and coming out hill just keeping it on the forefront of my mind and so that was that was a big thing for me this spring was um you anytime I got opportunity to to come down hill and run through not just step down that was on the forefront of my mind. >> Is being a new dad change your approach how you lead or even come at the game at all? >> Um not as much as I thought it was. It did. It does a little bit in the fact that, you know, now that I have a son, you know, I look at things as, you know, I want, and I granted he's only five months old, so he's he's still little, you know what I mean? But, um, I just think of it as being a new dad. My actions and everything, I want to reflect so that when he gets older, he sees how I conduct myself as a man, as a husband, as a teammate, as whatever I'm doing. And so, um, that started to creep in a little bit. But, like I said, he's only five months now. He's he ain't crawling yet. He's starting to, but um but yeah, just hopefully that answers your question a little bit. >> Sol said that he thinks that one of your biggest attributes on the field is your instinctiveness. How do you feel like you develop that over the course of your career? >> Um I mean you you come with instincts like every player is different, right? I mean some people have a little bit more, some people have a little bit less. I think just my experience alone, you know, because I've been in it for eight years, like I said earlier, but um as you play, the more the more reps you get, the more instinct they kind of build. It's it's it's kind of like a gut feeling. If you're ever doing something, you kind of get that gut feeling. That's that's kind of what it's like. You know, if you're in a certain part of the field, you've been, oh, something something's probably coming behind me. It's more more of a gut feeling, I could say. But I think that I think that builds just with more experience and over time. >> I'm sure every defense ever played a stressed, fast, physical, violent. What is it about this group of coaches or this scheme that actually makes it the cornerstone rather than just a thing people stress? >> Because here it's more than just talking about it. It's becoming an identity and becoming part of the culture if that makes sense. >> Just by preaching non-stop and also on the field even though we don't have pads on. Um you know it's it's not just being physical. It's the the term we use is violent. And so it's not just being like we think of violent as just like hitting someone hard but it's not just that. violent out of your break, violent with your eyes, violent with your hands, violent with your intentions and being deliberate in the way you do things. >> You get a front row view of Jeff Simmons seeing him in this attacking scheme as opposed to two gap and all that. How much do you think he can impact this defense and and make your job easier, not easier, but make your job, you know, a better situation for you? >> Oh, it's going to be huge. I mean, that dude, as you guys know, Jeff is, you know, one of the best to do it and he's just going to be causing havoc every play and just letting him go versus just like you said versus two gap and he's just going to be just go, you know what I mean? >> How about just on the run defense? Before you got here, did you always consider that one of your strengths and it kind of slipped last year or what? >> Um, no, I I had a great year versus run in Denver. Um, and it was just, like I said, I'm not going to get into the ins and outs of it, but just overall I just felt like last year it was I felt like that aspect of my game was soft. That's the term I use for it. It just felt soft. And so, um, like I said, that's that's something that will improve this year. You know, I'm expecting to have a big year in the run game. And so, um, I think last year, Paul, we had a conversation around this time about pass versus run, that that kind of stuff. And um it's funny, the year before that it was the pass I was looking to improve on and then had a great year in the past. And so I'm a believer in what you emphasize you get out. And so um obviously I'm emphasizing the run game like I've said, but also just looking to emphasize just bringing all aspects of my game, not just you can't just focus on one thing and leave something you're good at behind. You know, you always got to look at all aspects of the game. >> You have you have the muscles last week. Did you do that now? >> No, I did it I did it Sunday and my I called my wife. if I facetime her cuz she's out of town and she's like, "What are you doing?" >> I appreciate you guys. Thank you. >> Congratulations.

title: Robert Saleh on Titans Minicamp, D-Line Rotation and the Next 40 Days
text: In when a read defense, when you're reading a quarterback in a defense, where's the biggest advantage for players and how much of it is a transition for them? Is it something that can be done quickly when you've been playing a match defense? >> Uh it's difficult to transition to either side, whether you've been a vision-based defense and then you're trying to go to match and vice versa. Um for us it's all going to tie into rushing coverage. You know, the faster the rush is, the more we the faster we can get our feet in the ground, the faster we can anticipate where the ball's going. Um it also dictates whether or not the coordinator and the quarterback can hold uh coordinator can call plays that are deeper developing and whether or not the quarterback can hold it. And so uh we'll get a really good feel for where we are from a defensive line standpoint with regards to the rush part of it. Um but the rushing coverage all tie together. >> As you begin to develop your plan for Jeffrey Simmons, how much do you feel his versatility is going to allow him to be able to move around and and do different things with >> Um he he he's capable of doing a lot. What what you guys are going to find with us is we don't we try not to move guys that much. We want them to master their skill. Like he's uh uh Jeffrey's an interior rusher. He's probably the best one one of the best arguably the best one of uh football and um our job is to find ways to get him one-on-ones. Uh and the more one-on-ones we can get him, the the more we're going to win. >> How much do you look back on things you did with Quinnen Williams and say I know I can do that with him in the box? >> Uh Sim, they're different. You know, Quinnen Quinnen is is outstanding in his own way. Um uh they're slightly different, but both equally effective. >> You guys have talked a lot about the plans you have for Femi and how to use him and convert him to a hand-in-the-dirt end, but we haven't been able to see him out here at all. Is he still is he healthy? Is he dealing with injuries? >> He's nursing an injury. >> You talked about Cam being better in the move the ball period. We saw that again yesterday. Um how much might you be crafting Cam with move the ball in in mind? How much more hopeful >> That's >> a good question. You guys are going to see it all the day. Today uh last day of mini camp, we're putting the ball down and everything's going to be move the ball kind of scrimmage like phase three rules. And we're going to we try to transition to that. I you know, in traditionally, you've got your team run and your seven-on-seven and what you guys have kind of seen. Um we're not going to operate that way during training camp. It's going to be more move the ball, more situation-based, more random in terms of what happens with the play and one for the play caller, two for the players so they can learn how to play the game of football or acclimate themselves to to playing the game of football. So, when we do get the game time, we're ready for it. But Go ahead. No, you >> You'd be better at that. Seems like everybody would be better at that. I mean, is that the closest you can come >> Yeah, when you when when you don't have a chance to overthink the script in my opinion, you know, you get the script and you read it and you got all these plays and sometimes you can kind of uh uh predetermine what you want to do on that particular play. You're trying to envision something and uh but when it's given to you and you've got the 40-second play clock and you've got to make a decision and you just got to play the game, a lot of these guys just show up. So, like I've said all along, Cam has been outstanding in all these move the ball periods. Um and looking forward to seeing how this this little mini scrimmage turns out. >> I know it's early, but what's the balance been for you play calling and head coaching responsibilities this time around? I know that that wasn't as much of an emphasis for you last time. >> Uh no, for sure. It's it's fine. You know, like calling the defense is um I think calling an offense and then dealing having to do with like two-minute timeouts and all that is probably a little bit more difficult than calling a defense. Usually, I'm on the other side just uh if that makes sense. But but it's it's fine. I feel like we've been calling defense for a long time. We should be able to do it. >> What have you seen from some of the depth receiver guys? KJ, some of the undrafted guys, Bryce is kind of competing >> No, there is a it's a it's going to be a fierce competition on the uh uh for those uh for those final receiver spots. Uh really good depth in those rooms. I think Aussie's doing a really nice job. Um looking forward again like Kinsey X, all those guys, it's it's going to be a fierce competition come training camp. Um and once we get the pads on, it'll be interesting to see who separates themselves. >> Getting back to Jeff, how is that conversation been as far as the the rotation and him what is it 60%? I think he's he's typically 80 to 90%. So, how is that conversation? >> No, um uh we haven't we haven't quite had it yet, but uh you know, it's I and I I I've said it like the if if if there's a 60-play game and Jeffrey plays 40 of them, the hope is that it was 40 passes. >> Okay. >> You know, like that that's the goal. Uh to get him doing what he does at Now, he can defend the heck out of the run and he's probably one of the better run defenders, too. So, he of course he's going to defend the run, but the whole point of the rotation is to make sure that Jeffrey Simmons is ready for that one-on-one when we need it. Third down, 2-minute, he's fresh, he's ready to roll, um and ready to exert every last fiber in his body in winning that one-on-one. So, that's that's really the purpose behind it. >> Is there a world where he could show you that he could play more than the percent that or the amount of snaps? >> Um I guess, but I I've said it before like if if he's able to go 50 plays out of 60, he's not doing it right. >> Is he dealing with something where you just decided to be super careful with him? >> Uh yeah, he's dealing with a couple things. >> What's Cody Barton kind of showing you from this position from where he was a big leader in that in that room last year? Has he continued that? >> Yeah, he's uh you know, he uh if you're familiar with where he got drafted, he was very similar system. Um uh we've evolved a little bit from where uh when he got in the league in Seattle, but uh still similar principles. So, he's he it's like riding a bike, man. He's been really, really good. He's got great command of the huddle. Doing really good at the line of scrimmage in terms of communicating and making the adjustments that need to be made with as the offense shifts and moves. So, I I think he's done a really nice job. >> In your opinion, what's his biggest strength? >> He's very instinctive. Very and a great communicator. >> You guys have a lot of receivers in on this roster right now that are sort that are on the smaller side. What's the advantage that those guys have being able to use, I guess, their their speed rather than their height? >> Yeah, and and and the quickness part, but I I think we've got a really good mix, you know? You look at Reed, you look at Tate, Alec, DK. Like they're bigger receivers. And then Wan'Dale and Kinsey and X. Kind of more of the shifty guys in the slot and even uh Ozzie and I'm sure I'm forgetting a couple. Like I feel like there's a little bit of everything and and it's really good with Daboll and his staff, you know, coming from those New England trees. They had a little bit of everything, too, from the West Welkers to the Randy Mosses and you know, so [clears throat] they're they're experienced in how to utilize those different body types, those different skill sets and how they're how to implement them within the scheme. So, they're they all have a home, they all have a skill set and you know, knock on wood for Daves, he'll know exactly how to get it get it out of them. >> I know I know you'll know a lot more than Pat's coming up. I wonder what you look for from the offensive and defensive line at this stage of the off season and what are you saying to those guys? >> Um honestly, I I want to see them show up, you know? Just be here, work your tail off in individual, know what you're supposed to do with regards to the half speed, the three-quarter stuff that we're doing on the offensive and defensive line during the 11-on-11 periods. Um but I I promise you it's going to crank up a hundredfold once the season starts. >> How do you envision your fourth and fifth receiver? Outside of putting pressure on on the guys ahead of them, what kind of snaps will they get coming in in in relief and kind of how do you characterize them? I'm not there to answer that question yet. I still want to see it cuz it's I mean your fourth and fifth receivers might not be worthy of a snap. Not saying that our guys are that, but it's still you there's still a long way to go to decide that. Um obviously they've got to have they've got to have great versatility. I do know that cuz they've got to be able to play all three spots. They've got to be great special teamers because of the fact that their snaps will be down. So there's a long way to go to decide all that stuff, but really when you're looking at that four-five spot, you're looking for more versatility um in terms of the different positions they can play in special teams value. >> How helpful of a player has Tony been to get guys in the right position? >> He's been great. The same thing, you know, he's he knows our system. He's been helpful. He's a you know, Tony's an energy giver. Um I know he wasn't out there yesterday. He came down with a little stomach, but hopefully he's feeling better this morning, but uh um he's an absolute energy giver. He's very smart. He's communicates very well and uh um just thankfully he's here. >> What's the balance between getting away and clearing your mind a little bit and then also being ready for when camp starts? And how do you advise guys in all that? >> Coach's standpoint or player? >> Well, I guess both. Yeah. Yeah, I guess both. Yeah. >> Coach? Uh I'll be taking a lot of naps on the beach hopefully with the with the kids if they let me, but uh and golfing. But no uh it's more important for the player um cuz our minds we're always going to be connected to the building. I'll still come in here during those 40 days and get some uh stuff done and organize things for uh training camp, um you know, and and I'll talk to the players more about it uh uh tomorrow, but these next 40 days are are critical and I and I feel like so many players lose their season before it ever starts because of the way they handle these next 40. It's not a vacation. Um they've got to get ready to play ball. You know, we we kind of trick trick it by pretending the four-day acclimation period will help them kind of give them a runway to get into the season. That there is no runway. Um, when you get here, we got to go and and if you're not prepared to play, you're going to get hurt. And that's just that's league-wide. And and we can put bubble wrap on these guys and and delay the inevitable, which leads to injury weeks 1 through 5 during the season, but the important thing is that our players attack the heck out of the next 40 days, get here ready to play, and have an amazing training camp. Yeah, it's uh it's all conditioning level, you know, like um there's you know, our strength crew put together a great program for them over the next 40 days to to get them ready for that first day of practice. And then from there, the acclimation and the build-up will continue to rise. Um, but a lot of the soft tissue injuries come in because they're not prepared for the load that that they're going to get hit with or and I get it. You're going to go out, you're going to enjoy your vacation, you're going to go to the beach, you're going to have some drinks, and all that stuff. But you've got to be mindful about what you're doing to your body and and how you're preparing yourself to play cuz one injury, you set yourself back 2 weeks. I mean, you just take our situation and our schedule. A week and a half in the camp, we're having a scrimmage in the uh in the stadium. Two weeks from report day, we're in San Francisco practicing and we're playing a game. So, you got 2 weeks. Um, four a four-day acclimation period is not covering that. So, you've got to be able to prepare in a way that uh that that has you ready from from from day one. And so, like I said, we've got a a great program that we've put together for the guys to follow. Um, and they're always welcome to do more than what's being asked. >> Robert, the philosophy you've developed with deploying your defensive lineman, where does that come from? Is there like an influence that you've pulled from just in how just how how how you've wanted that to look? >> Yeah, you know, in 2019 we made a shift from playing six technique and the you know, the the old school 4-3 stuff. Brought in Chris Kaseric who is a disciple of Washburn who was here for a long time and those great D-lines. So, we run a similar system to that and the the the demand at which we ask the the things that we ask out of our D-line, the the the the strain, the grind, the violence, the speed at which we ask them to play, it's it's just impossible for them to be able I mean I mean I guess it's not impossible. I mean be the bionic man, but it's it's it's hard. It's hard. If you're doing it the right way, it's hard to be able to go four plays in a row, let alone 80%. So, the idea behind it though is to just make sure that we have That's it's why we have so many D-linemen, that we have our guys as fresh as possible, so we're constantly able to throw our hardest pitch at those old linemen. And as they stand there for 70 plays in a game, you just keep getting a new fresh body every play just punching you in the mouth over and over and over and over again to the point to where that fourth quarter rolls around, hopefully we wore you out. >> Last one. Robert, a lot has been made of Cam's mindset. Yesterday, he kind of mentioned, you know, he's not big on complimenting himself. Is that sustainable in your opinion, or can he benefit from maybe relishing in some of the positives of this? >> Um No, I I think that's what drives him. I I do think it's important for self-affirmation of giving yourself a pat on the back once in a while and accepting some praise, but but I also think the three most dangerous words in life are I got it. And um you know, and and the most important thing you do as a as a competitor, you just got to avoid the big meal, you know, just and I think that's what's good about him is he's he wants to be the best in the world, but at the same time if he's a true competitor, he's never going to see him in that light he's see him see himself in that light. He's always going to be able to find something that he can get better at and I think that's what you want from all our athletes. >> Thanks everyone for your >> Thank you guys.

title: Greg Lewis, Shea Tierney and Titans Coaches Meet with Media
text: I'm broke. >> undersized receivers on the roster. What's the What's it like to employ those guys versus the guys who go up and, you know, maybe win the contested catches and that sort of thing. What's What's the key to employing those guys correctly? >> Well, it's just our job as as coaches to evaluate what we have skill set wise and put them in position to do different things. So, you have your contested catch type of guys and then you have your guys that separate and then you got guys that possibly can do both. And you just try to find a way to put them in position to best help the offense and be successful and move the chains and and make plays. So, I think we got a lot of different body types, a lot of different types of guys offensively at the receiver position. And we just try to move everybody around, get a feel for what they're doing. It's been a great spring for that. And we're looking forward to to training camp and moving forward with everybody we got. >> Who would you say are the things you maybe you preach the most for what you want your group to be known for at practice and games? >> Making plays. That's our job is is to make the quarterback's job easy. So, when we get opportunities to make plays for the quarterback, we got to take advantage of those type of opportunities. And then just a mindset of a dog mentality. Just being disciplined, being attention to detail, having a good attitude, work ethic, grit and just being smart players when we're on the field. Relentless is is my mindset of how I coach and how I approach these guys. And you just try to find a way to put them in position because you have to be relentless to to be a good professional football player, whether you're playing receiver or whether you're playing any other position. So, the guy across from you is relentless and you have to match it and then exceed that. >> If you look at last year, this group they had big time struggles against press coverage. What can you do to help improve that this year and make it a better situation for your quarterback? >> Well, we're just trying to work on releases as much as possible daily. Uh talking about the small details with the guys, whether it's out on the field correcting something that I see out there, or we get into the film room uh working on those type of things. Those type of releases or those coaching points uh inside the film room. But, I think all the guys here have taken a step in the right direction uh from a release standpoint and winning against press coverage, tight man coverage, uh match type of coverage. And we're just going to continue to build off that. I I think the guys here, the one thing that I I truly do love about this group of guys that I have is that they love football. They love the game of football. They love the small details of being a professional athlete, and they understand it's their job, and they want to get better. They're sponges about trying to find all the details including press coverage uh of how to get better and how to make us a better team. >> What's the key to uh advancing Carnell kind of as quickly as you can, to be as effective as you can, as fast as you can? >> I mean, just studying. I mean, that that's any job that you have. Uh you you got to be a master of your craft and understanding, and you got to put in the time and the effort to to be better, to get better, and do the things. Carnell has done a a tremendous job uh of understanding this offense, learning the the the ins and outs of what we need and what we're asking him to do at his position. And all the guys have have done that. So, it's it's just about study habits, and then it's about taking the meeting room to the practice field, and then taking the practice field to the game field. Uh with with all these guys. And and Carnell is no exception. He's done a a tremendous job, as have all the other guys that are involved with the receiving room. >> How would you describe how Ridley's attacked this offseason and attacked his rehab? Just where is he at right now? >> Well, honestly, I'm not a doctor, so I I can't sit up here and tell you uh rehab-wise or this, that, and the third. I can tell you that he's been a great leader uh in our room. Uh obviously being uh the longest-tenured player in the NFL, he's seen a lot, he's done a lot, he's been successful, and he's imparting some of that wisdom that he has from off the field and on the field stuff to the younger guys and developing help develop those guys. And then he's getting back with with coach Davis who he had at Alabama, and he's understanding the offense, and then he's going out there and he's doing his job. >> A lot of the younger guys they they mentioned last year his intensity like it rubs off on them. Is that something you've noticed? Like how much do you think the way he practices can help a young guy like like I am matter like like tape like DK? >> I I believe energy is contagious and it could come from anybody. Obviously Ridd practices hard every day that he's out there. Uh, all the guys do. That that like I said earlier, like this group of guys love football and they attack each day with a mindset of getting better, bringing energy, bringing physicality, competing, and doing different things which is a collective group and if we get everybody doing that which we have, all right, that just makes everybody better in the whole entire group. >> How much of a resource has Rondale been for the group as someone who who has spent so much time with with Davis in in terms of what he's trying to do here in Tennessee? >> Uh, he's been a tremendous resource. Not not only for the players but the coaches and that and that goes back with with Belly, uh, with Mitch and all those guys that have been in the system before. Obviously it's a new learning system for everybody uh, that hasn't been in it. So being able to lean on those guys that have been in the offense, know the nuances of the offense, know the ins and outs, it's been tremendous in our room obviously for the receivers. Uh, and I think those guys have sprinkled around and talked to everybody as far as what the expectation is, how we do things, how how Davis certainly wants different things and different routes and different concepts. And I I think it's been a a great help for the entire offense and it has expedited uh, the process for us as far as being able to pick up and then go out and execute uh at a high level. >> You got to see those Kansas City offenses take off in real time. >> Yeah. Are there any traits that you can identify that you can bring with you from that of kind of transferring that success to here? Is there something or was it kind of magic? >> I don't know. I I want to say it's it's it's magic um being being out there and that that's my former life. Being there part of those uh championship teams was great. Um but I think we have the people in place here to continue to go out and get better each day and put it on tape when we get out in into the season and we see what we got from there. >> What do you think about >> uh chairman Elam and their rookie seasons and what are ways they can can get better? >> Uh I I thought they had their their ups and their downs as do all rookies in in involved in in in NFL. Uh I think that they can work on football, being a receiver, being a complete receiver as far as being able inside, play outside, understanding route, uh understanding coverages and different things of that nature so they can put it all together and then go out and play fast and and make plays. But I think both of those guys have tremendous upside. Um they they're great workers. They want to get better um and and and they're doing everything possible uh to to make that happen. >> Thanks, coach. Appreciate >> Explain where the ball's laying out in front of them and they're laying down and then they pick it up and throw it in the net. Can you kind of explain to us the meaning behind that drill? >> It's just a competition drill we done all the way back to uh Buffalo. Um just something to get them started at the beginning of practice to get the competitive juices flowing. Um more more so that than anything technique-wise or anything like that. Um has nothing to do with really playing quarterback in terms of throwing and all that. Just hey, we're getting competitive juices flowing. Let's see who can get up the fastest, throw the ball to the square on point at the quickest and win the drill. >> Yesterday's with the with the ball coming over the quarterback's head short distance to find it. >> Yeah, I think that was Cam just going over there and having fun. Um if we ever have to throw him a pass, hopefully that drill shows up. >> [laughter] >> How's How's How's Cam been I guess from time you first got your hands on him to leaving here after tonight? >> Uh really good. I'm I'm really happy with just the way Cam overall approaches the game and the meetings and the whole process of being a quarterback. Uh you know, I can go back to our first week of uh the veteran mini camp that we had. Um you know, it's like 5:45 in the morning. Um I'm just kind of getting ready for my day and I get a call from him and he's talking about an adjustment on a play that we actually talked about as a coaching staff the day before and I hadn't even talked to him about it yet. And he was already thinking about making that adjustment with us. And that's in the first week we're not really together. So, just to have him there already kind of in our first week together of thinking of those things just showed me that we have a guy who's really committed to the game, um is always thinking about it and really just has that hunger to be great, which is what you want to start with with your quarterback. >> You guys got to spend a lot of time with him leading into last year, the draft and everything. But what have you learned new about Cam Ward now that you spent time like actually in the room and and coaching? >> Um probably just what I I referenced there because even in that process you get a sense for how serious they take it and how committed they are to their craft. But when you get to spend time with them in the meeting room and then you get the calls outside of the meeting room, you get the calls and texts in the morning, you really you really see it. Um, anybody going through that process can I don't want to say fake it, but you know, they could show it a little bit and you think they have it, but until you get your hands on them and you're around them for an extended period of time, you don't know that. Um, so so Cam's commitment to the game and commitment to being a great quarterback is really awesome. You know, just a guy who who really puts the work in. Um, which is which is what you want. >> What are some of the adjustments that quarterbacks have to make? This team's got several guys who are undersized receivers like Wan'Dale, Restrepo, Kinsey-Doll. What's the adjustment that quarterbacks have to make to throw to those guys versus somebody that's like a 6'3" or 6'4" guy? >> Yeah. That's a That's a good question and I think it doesn't necessarily go into the size of them. Um, 6'3" guys as opposed to Wan'Dale who's who's a little smaller or Restrepo like you said, we always kind of put them in categories of you know, separators or contested guys. And a lot of the times you find those smaller guys are are the separators. So, there's a bigger target area to hit for them because there's more space. And then the bigger guys are sometimes more contested catch guys. So, what you say with them sometimes is, "Hey, they're covered but they're not covered." Because of their wingspan, because of their physicality. Um, so I think that's more of how we we talk about it in terms of do they separate or are they more contested catch players rather than their size? >> Do you have to like adjust the play calls if they're if the smaller guys are in there and and not throw a jump ball in the corner of the end zone, that sort of thing. >> I don't think it's necessarily the play call. I think it's within the play of what routes you have guys on. You know, you know you're not going to put a guy on a contested catch route that that's not his strength. So, we try to do as good a job as we can of putting our guys in the best position to make those plays and use their strengths and kind of stay away from some of the things they don't do as well. So, it does go into the play call, but more specifically the route we're asking them to run in that play call. So, I mean, if I gave you the playbook here, you guys can spend five days looking at it and there's we could come up with a million different route combinations for that, right? But when we do narrow it down to the 15 or 20 that we want to work on for that day, okay, is this route good for player X? Yes, it is. Keep him on that. All right, we have this play call. Is this route good for player Y? It's probably not the best route for him to run. Let's change it to this. So, it goes in more into that. Yes, but that's before we get out here. We know who's going to be in in each personnel grouping. So, we're trying to put those guys in the best position to accentuate their strengths. >> Are you some Are you someone who believes that accuracy can be improved through coaching? >> 100% >> Not that uh he was inaccurate, but I was there for the start of Josh's career in Buffalo and you could see the accuracy on film in um Wyoming. And it's like I referenced a couple weeks ago with that is just how do you make it more consistent? So, there are different drills you can do. There's different um thought processes you can have with it when you come out at the start of the day to do that. Um you never want to make it where they're thinking about it while they're playing the game. It's more of an indie thing. It's more of an off-season thing. But 100% I I think you can. Um I think every quarterback can get more accurate just by watching video of their mechanics down the line in a slow-mo type environment, talking about those things with each throw, whether it was a good throw or a bad throw. You could point out, "Hey, this is why this ball went where you wanted it to. Hey, this is why the ball kind of sailed a little bit on you." And just making guys more conscious of that helps number one, and then going out and drilling it helps, too. >> How much do you think play calling cuz I've been watching this a lot seem like there's a lot of high percentage throws built in for him. How much do you think that could help the accuracy as well? >> Well, I I think you know, you're getting into a discussion really that's what type of play are you trying to What's the intent of the play, right? So, when we have a play called, when Dave sends in a play, we know what we're trying to get done. Are we trying to take a shot? Are we trying to hit it downfield, which is obviously when you're throwing it downfield, lower percentage, right? Um is it intermediate? So, are we trying to get a chunk? Or is it a short one where we're just trying to get the ball out of our hands and completing the ball to basically augment the run game. You know, like that's what you're trying to do with some of those. So, does that help drive completion percentage up? Yes. That doesn't necessarily mean your accuracy's better because you're calling a high completion per play, and now we're hitting 75% of our passes, and everybody thinks, "Oh, he's got 75%. He's accurate." That's not always the case. An accurate passer to me is somebody who um execute the intent of the play call and hit what we're trying to hit. And if we're hitting those spots that we're trying to hit based on the play call, that's an accurate passer. Completion percentage is it lies a lot. you know, like I said, not to reference um the past, but you know, guys who have had less than 60% completion percentage in college have come into the NFL and now all of a sudden they're completing 67% of their passes. Like there's not just the accuracy plays into that, but what are they trying to do in the play call to get that up to? >> Is that basically what you mean when you say accuracy on film? Like you look at Josh in college and the difference between him a guy that you saw accuracy on film versus a guy that maybe had the same completion percentage in college, but you'd watch his tape and say, I don't see that accuracy on film. Is it because of the the different things they were being asked to do? Is it >> I it's a combination. Um some guys will, you know, you can as you watch and evaluate a quarterback, certain themes show up, right? So, you know, it's a very extensive process we have to break down a quarterback's accuracy and what they've done in college to evaluate them. We separate the fields into different uh yardages, separate the fields into different quadrants going left to right, and we track all of those. Um and then when there's a lower completion percentage in one of those areas, okay, let's go look at that first. Why is he got a lower completion percentage in this area? Like like left middle as opposed to right deep. All right, why? All right, if you have a quarterback where the completion percentage is low in, you know, let's just call it four of the six areas, all right, there's probably some inaccuracy issues there. So, can they be fixed then? Well, that goes into a whole 'nother deal of when you get around them, are they flexible? What's their base like? You know, there's a the ton of layers to that. But to start, you break it down into that and that gives you a sense of all right, well he's really accurate in four areas, two areas he's not. Maybe that is what they were asked to do. Maybe that, you know, there were three drops in that area and that's why that percentage is lower, right? So you're always trying to go through those with a fine-tooth comb and figure out the reasons why. Number one, was it scheme, receiver, throw, play call, all of that, defense, right? Did he throw it into the to the wrong look? Like that's also completion percentage. The He would have completed the ball if he went to the right spot, but you know, it wasn't inaccurate, it was a bad decision. So it's a very comp- completion percentage is a very, very uh broad topic, I think. >> Appreciate it, coach. >> Appreciate it. >> Thanks, guys. >> When you're on ground and getting guys in the early individuals to jump off the ball, uh why are you down on the ground? Uh is there not another tool that you could use or you could just like seeing that angle? >> Uh as as much as anything, we're just working on distraction. I I want them to get really focused in on whatever implement, whatever apparatus we're using that day to get off the ball. And so I whatever we can do to change it up, keep it interesting, but still make it there's all this stuff going on around you, but you still got to focus in on the ball and getting off on the ball, that's the purpose of it. And some of it's silly, some of it's overdone, but like I just really want there to be a lot of chaos, but to still be able to focus in on getting off on the ball. >> I know Robert said Femi's kind of dealing with something else keeping him from practice. What are some things he's been able to do during the course of the off season that will help him when camp starts? >> Well, he he's been here since day one and he's been working and working and working and even though he had, you know, the slight nicks and stuff that he's working through right now, uh we've we've got a lot of made a lot of progress in really just um defining who he is as a rusher and who he is as a defensive end versus some of the things that he's done in the past, which are are are different, but they're not wrong, they're just different. And and just defining what that looks like for him and his body style and his talents. And um he's done a really great job of just uh soaking up that information and really making it, you know, we're all individuals, but we have a common goal. And so it's like you're taking your individual talents and working it into that common goal, and he's done great with that. >> When you have a guy like that transitioning to a new position, how much does like with this scheme simplifying and just allowing him just attack and not have to read so much, like how much will that help him make that transition and play better? >> Yeah, I I think the biggest thing is for all of these guys, and this is not just just Femi, is for any of us, whatever our job is in here. We all have different titles and stuff, but for any of us to be successful, we got to know what's expected of us. So if we don't know what the expectations are, like this is good, this is where the standard is, this is what we need to get to, we can't be at our best. And so for Femi, for everybody else is learning what the expectations are, what do what is the standard that's set in this room, how do we want it to look, and then I put my own personal spin on it. Like the way you write an article is not going to be the same as she writes an article and that right, but there's still a standard of hey, this is the journalism standard that we're trying to follow right here. >> Obviously the understanding is that you want all your guys to be able to defend the run and the pass, but Robert was telling us about how if there's a 60-play game, Jeff ideally plays 40 snaps and all 40 of them are are pass downs. So if if if you're going to maximize him as a pass rusher, who are the guys in your group that are going to be maximized as run defenders? >> I Well, I as a run defender, everybody's got to stop the run because for you to get 40 passes in a game, you better stop the run. So, it don't matter as if if we got 10 people up on game day, 9 8 7 6 5 4 3 2 1, if they're not trying to stop the run, they ain't going to pass the ball. If they can keep handing it off for five, it don't matter. So, I I think as a group collectively, we got to do that to give ourselves opportunities to get those one-on-ones. You earn one-on-ones by getting to those pass downs and and it's a full team game. It's a team defensive game, but as a group it starts with that. >> What specifically have you seen from Keldrick from the start of this to to sending him off for the summer? >> I I think the biggest thing is no different than Femi is understanding the expectations, understanding the technique and the standards as full as the group is the scheme is different from Auburn. The expectations are different from Auburn. And again, Auburn's not wrong, it's just different. And so, for those guys to come in and learn and then, you know, for all of all of young players in the NFL this is not just unique to Keldrick or Jackie is rushing the passer in the NFL is a totally different ballgame than college football. And and there's these guys these guys are blocking you, they're good. They were the best at their college and you got to take your game to another level. >> A guy like Jermaine Johnson who's now in his second year coming back from a torn Achilles, are you a subscriber to the fact that second to the belief that second year from back from an injury a lot of times guys are more more closer to what they were before? >> I would be speaking out of ignorance on that in terms of like what the data says on stuff like that. You know, what I can say is that I'm excited where Jermaine's at, what I'm seeing out on the practice field and in individual has me it reminds me of what I've seen before in the past from him, which is part of the reason why Mike and and Robert brought him here. And I'm just thankful that he's here and that I feel like he is the guy that that I remember from the Jets. >> What was the actual process of the D-line rotation work on game days? What's gone well for the new coaches that were onboarding here? the um coaches that are all now part of a new system offensively and defensively. What have we liked? What could we learn? How would we do it differently? And so having the ability to give feedback to one another, like that's a learned skill. and you trust that even if it's someone that is technically below you on the the ladder that that you're going to get the honesty that that you need so that you can make sure going into 2026 >> you can be a better version of yourself as an NFL head coach. >> And I've come to recognize after, you know, maybe, you know, going on to like nine years as a head coach, sometimes it's not me they don't want to give feedback to, it's the seat, >> you know, of the head coach or going into there. So, I try to make it where, hey, um, Donte, David, let's let's split this up as a staff. Let's have a breakout with these two or three people.
